maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Rule 39, for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the lifting of the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway west of Edmonton, now in progress.
And leave having been granted.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the subject matter of this motion relates to a part of the country very distant from the Capital, I hope it is not considered to be less important by the people of this part of Canada than it is by those in the part of Canada directly affected. This matter has been brought to my attention by urgent telegrams, one from the Jasper Park collieries, which I read to the House yesterday, and the other from the secretary of the Board of Trade of the town of Edson. Both the Jasper Park colleries and^the town of Edspn are very intimately and directly affected by the action now being taken. It is nearly six months since notice was first given in the newspapers that the Government intended taking this action. That announcement naturally aroused considerable interest, especially amongst the people most directly affected. When the House was convened in January I t.ook the liberty of asking my friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) if such action were contemplated, and was informed by him, if I remember correctly, that it was not. The people then rested easy and were satisfied that no such action was intended. It was a shock to them to learn that it was definitely and deliberately intended that the means of communication upon which they depended, the existence of which alone made it possible for them to be where they were and to do 'business, was about to he t,aken away from them without consideration of any kind whatever, and without information to the public or to the Parliament of this country. While I 
do not wish to speak in a controversial tone on this occasion, I am bound to say that I do not think it right that this country of Canada and the people of Canada should be governed in that way. Surely when, for. good or bad reason, it is intended by the Government of the country to absolutely destroy the value of the property owned by citizens of this country, to -take from them the returns upon the time they have employed in their present location, the least that these people and the country at large are entitled to its information as to how, when and why, the reasons for such action in absolute detail. This House of Commons, representing the people of this country, are entitled to that information at the hands of this Government. I am sorry to say that when I brought- the matter to the attention of the hon. minister yesterday in the terms of a most urgent telegram from an enterprise that depends upon its -business for its profits and to which a delay of only one day means a very considerable financial loss, I was given very little satisfaction.. This House and this country are entitled to more than a general statement that this company is -going to be taken care of; it is entitled to know how this company is going to be -taken care of and when it is going to be taken care of. The amount of money that is invested in- this enterprise is sufficiently great to mean -that a large number of citizens are affected, and every man knows that in the case of an industrial enterprise of this character, any action that has the effect of discrediting -that enterprise certainly must have an injurious effect upon the investment of capital in it. So the least the Government can- do when it is taking such action is, by giving the fullest possible -information at the earliest possible date, to minimize the loss by eliminating uncertainty. The Jasper Park colleries is an enterprise which was undertaken at the time of the construction of the Grand Trunk railway. The collieries are located absolutely on the line of the railway, they are most conveniently situated. The coal is of a character suitable for locomotive purposes and the enterprise of the collieries is absolutely dependent upon the enterprise of the railway, partly for the coal sold to the Tailway company for use in its locomotives, and partly by reason of the facilities afforded by the railway for the transportation of coal to other customere.

On the main line of the
Grand Trunk Pacific railway. It is so fortunately situated that in the earlier stages of development it was possible to chute the coal down into the cars of the railway company. There is no doubt that the convenience of location was in large measure the inducement to people to invest their money in the enterprise, and when this Government, in broad, general terms, announces that as a part of its policy those rails are to be tom up and does not vouchsafe to this House or any one else any suggestion ias to what else is being done in the matter, I say it is deliberately undertaking to wreck an important industrial enterprise in the province of Alberta-and that is not the business of any Government, no matter who is its leader or who compose it.
This subject has been before the public in the eastern press for a considerable period, and in order that the House may understand the facte, I shall have to ask the liberty of trespassing for a few moments to explain the actual situation. I have seen statements in the press that for two or three hundred miles the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern railway were duplicated, occupying the same territory, and without any reason for two lines of railway. In this particular case I want to say that the Jasper Park Collieries are situated at the foot of Mount Miette, one of the outer chain of the Rockies, on the south side of the Atha-baska river. The valley of the Atha-baska river forms the eastern part [DOT] of *what is generally known as the Yellowhead pass, and gives entrance from the prairies into the mountains from the east side. It happens that the Athabaska river at that point is spread into a lake, or rather a series of lakes, Jasper lake and Brule lake, so it is not a matter merely of crossing the river but, if there is to be communication across the river, a matter of bridging several miles, which, of course, would be quite impossible. These lakes run for a length of a little over thirty miles, and it happens that the Grand Trunk Pacific goes up on the one side of these lakes and the Canadian Northern railway on the other, so that when the Grand Trunk track i6 taken away, as it is being taken away, there is no question that the Jasper Park colleries are left absolutely in the air. Commercially, they might as well be in Palestine as where they are. I have seen the suggestion that where the Government is going to tear up the Grand Trunk Pacific tracks-and where they are needed, if
you please-the rails are to be replaced by Canadian Northern rails that are to be taken up. The Canadian Northern runs for thirty odd miles on one side of the Athabaska river and the lakes, and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other. The Jasper Park colleries are on the south side, and the Grand Trunk Pacific depends largely on these collieries for its supply of fuel. Colleries are being developed on the other iside of the lake, one set by the Canadian Northern and another by the Jasper Park Colleries company, so that no one line of railway can by any possibility develop the coal properties on each aide of the Athabaska vallley in that stretch of the road. When the proprietors of the Jasper Park colleries see the track being taken up, they are told in a most indefinite way that they are going to be taken care of- though they know that the removal of the Canadian Northern tracks on the. other side would leave the collieries there in exactly the same position. I submit that the answer given to the question of the Jasper Park Colleries company regarding . the removal of these rails' is not by iany means satisfactory.
I have received telegrams not only from the Jasper Park colleries, but also from the town of Edson, which is a divisional point on the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, 130 miles west of Edmonton. It is the starting point of a provincial wagon road to Grand Prairie, and it has roundhouses and all the equipment of a divisional point. Two brajich railroads communicate with coal mines west of Edson, so that Edson takes care of the traffic not only on the main lines, but on these two branches which form a junction with the main line a little west of the town, at a place called Bickerdike-Which makes the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal', famous. The population of Edison is 600. The assessed value of the land in the town is over $1,000,000; its public buildings are worth $100,000 and other buildings $250,000. It has a debenture debt of $80,000. Surrounding the town of Edson is a rural municipality with 300 voters and with an assessment of $283,000. Beyond the municipality is a settlement which includes over 1,000 people, who settled there in the express understanding and belief that they were to have the l>enefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway as their means of communication. While there are portions of the line between Edmonton and Tete Jaune Cache where the two railways are very close

speechtext: Which one is that?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I could not make the
distinction. The Canadian Pacific has a double track from Port Arthur eastward. They were going to dtouble track it all the way to Montreal, and they got it partially ooimpieted before the slump came before the war. Then they ceased' construction, and the rails of that double track road are lying there still. The taking up of those rails would not affect injuriously the interests of any private citizen. It would, of course, be to- the disadvantage of the Canadian Pacific, but the Canadian Pacific has other lines, and I submit that until they find it necessary to double track all the way through, that portion of the road is of minor importance and of minor usefulness. But we do not lay hands on the Canadian Pacific. It seems that the rails of the Canadian Pacific are bored a little differently from the rails of the Grand Trunk, although both are of the same quality and weight of -steel.
The Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific are parallel from the foot of Kamloops . Lake to Yale in British Columbia, a distance of over 100 miles. Does the presence of those two roads increase the development of that part of the country? Why no one who has ever gone through that section would ever suggest such an absurdity. Is there so much traffic over these two roads that one road cannot carry it all? That is not true, either. I am reminded also that from Port Arthur to Nipigon the Canadian Northern and Canadian Pacific are parallel, and the Canadian Pacific is double-tracked for that distance

if I am not mistaken. There is no development there, and no possibility of development here or hereafter, now or in the future. So I say the conclusion is absolutely irresistible that this attach upon the Grand Trunk west of Edmonton is simply an attack upon the enterprise, and is made not with regard to the interests of the British Government and not in the interests of winning the war. It. is not fair dealing as between the people that are affected, and the people that would be affected by the lifting of rails in other parts of the country. But because these rails are out in Alberta or in the Rocky Mountains, because they are not in the great province of Ontario, it does not matter. I hope we have a House of Commons here that is a House of Commons for Canada, and not a House of Commons for any one province of Canada; a House of Commons that realizes that the growth of Canada depends upon the growth of every part of this country and that connection through the Rocky Mountains by the best possible pass is an absolutely necessary factor in the development of this country both east and west of the mountains.
We are told that these tracks must be torn up in order to win the war; that these rails are required in France, and therefore they must be taken up at -once because rails cannot be got anywhere else. Now, first of all, I am going to make an assertion, and it is this: the rails that have already been taken up on the 300 miles of the eastern part of the Transcontinental are not yet in France, nor is there any possibility of their being in France for a very considerable period. If rails are wanted in France, I ask you, Sir, and I ask this House, if they cannot be got, just as rails can he got to be used on roads in the Dominion of Canada. A short time ago I asked this question:
1.	Are rails for renewal purposes now required on the Intercolonial Railway?
2.	Will the rails so required, in all or in part, be rolled at Sydney or Sault Ste. Marie, under arrangements with the Imperial Munitions Board ?
Mr. Cochrane:
1 Yes.
2. To be rolled at Sydney.
Now, if rails can be rolled at Sydney for the Intercolonial, I fancy they can be rolled at Sydney for use in France, if it is desired to roll them at that point. But never mind about Sydney. There are on the other side of the line enormous plants for the production of railway material, including rails, and every man knows that it is only a ques-

tion of price whether those rails can be procured or not. If the price of rails to-day is $40 a ton, and rails cannot be got at that money, is there anybody who will say that they could not be got for $80 a ton on the other side of the line?

speechtext:
My hon. friend has my answer already. I saw in yesterday's papers that the Russian Government is able to make a contract with firms in the United States for supplying locomotives. Could not they have made a contract for an equal value of steel rails if they had paid the price? I think they could. My hon. friend mentions $100 a ton. I ask you, Sir, will $100 a ton pay the damages to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to my constituents, and to the people of Canada, resulting from the tearing up of these tracks? I say it will not begin to pay it, and an honest endeavour to do the best that could be done to help the war in France would have caused this Government to secure those rails from the United States at whatever price was necessary rathe: than tear up the rails in our own country, thereby discommoding our own people, discrediting our own enterprise, and in the end charging the British Government two or three times as much as they should have paid.
There are railways being built in Canada to-day, and there are many more that ought to be built. Rails are being bought for these railways. Rails are being laid now on a road 300 miles in length from Edmonton to Fort McMurray; were laid during the winter, and are being laid to-day. These rails were purchased somewhere, and I do not imagine that the management of that road have more resources with which to buy rails than has this Government. The Government is engaged in the construction of a railway on its own account, the Hudson Bay railway. We have been told that they have slackened construction on that road, that they are not going to push it to a finish. Well, if they are not going to push it to a finish, and at an early day too, I will ask these hon. gentlemen of what use under heaven are these rails that have already been laid, or the rails that are piled up ready to be used, but which will not be used? I am a supporter of the Hudson Bay
railway; I believe that that road should be pushed to completion, and pushed to completion at the earliest day. But if the Government is not going to use these rails for the Hudson Bay road, and is not going to finish the road, then why not use these rails instead of tearing up the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific west of Edmonton?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I am more than surprised at the extravagant statements made by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He seems to know more about what rails are required and what rails should go forward for use at the front than the British Government do. These rails are laid under fire in many cases, and the British
4 p.m. Government have asked us to send rails of the same borings and the same kind as before, so that they may be laid as easily and as quickly as possible. And now the statement is made again that we are bound to ruin the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and Transcontinental. It is all bosh-nothing but bosh. I have heard a great deal from the other side of the House to the effect that we have degraded the line and all that kind of thing. Why, that is all wrong; it is impossible. It is as good a road as ever has been laid; it has never been degraded in any sense of the word. I defy any one to prove it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Then why tear it up?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I would tear up the whole Transcontinental, yes, and every other railway in Canada, to win the war.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Then why would not the hon. gentleman take a few Canadian Pacific Railway rails?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Because, as I have told you, the British Government asked us to send rails of the same kind as those sent before. We sent over 300 miles of rails taken from the Transcontinental, taking up many of- the sidings, and rails in terminal points, which are not necessary at present, because they were laid to provide for a larger business than the road is likely to have for many a year.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Are not the railways in France on which these rails are being laid narrow gauge lines carrying light engines for the purpose of moving supply trains?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I do not know what railways they are used for-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: That is the statement made.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The statement made to us is that they want the same kind of rails that were sent before. The hon member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) tells the House, though he does not know anything about it, that the rails of the 300 miles already torn up have not been sent away. It is true they have not been sent across the ocean, but they are at Three Rivers, and the balance of them will go in a very short time. The authorities on the other side are urging us and cabling us day by day to get these rails ready at the seaboard, so that they may be got over as soon as transport can be furnished. The hon. member talks about the town of Edson. I have answered once before that I will look after the town of Edson.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: In what way?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I don't know. But I have two engineers out there who are laying out plans to that end, and they know more - about it than does my hon. friend from Edmonton. I have also said that the Jasper Coal Mines will be looked after. I cannot tell the House just, how, at this time, but I hope in a short time to have a map showing on paper exactly how the work will be carried on. I am not going to make a statement about something I do not know about. I am going to look after the different interests along that line, and I am going to carry out what the British Government want, no matter what it is.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: But you don't ask something from the Canadian Pacific Railway?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Because, I tell you, the Canadian Pacific Railway rails have different borings. I would like to send him to the front, by Heavens, to lay these rails.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I want him to understand that I am represented at the front. Is he?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I know you are, but you don't talk as if you were. The hon. gentleman's talk is for pure politics, and nothing else. He thinks his chances for re-election are so bad that he will have to make use of everything, turning this whole war into a political game, instead of fighting it out as he ought.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: That is what the Government has done from the start.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
No, they have not.
We had a lot of second-hand rails on the Intercolonial and Transcontinental, but we want to send over rails of the same kind as we sent before. We propose to take

care of every interest along these different roads. If we cannot do it altogether, then the British Government have agreed that they will look after any damage that may occur.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Have the Grand Trunk Pacific been consulted about this and have they consented? Have the bondholders consented as well?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
The Grand Trunk
Pacific has been asked.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The bondholders have a lien on these rails.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: But the Government are behind the guarantee, I am sorry to say.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I am afraid they will be behind it, if they take the bondholders' property without their consent.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I hope in a few days to be able to lay on the Table a map showing how we will be able to take care of the industries along the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern. This is going to cost some money but nothing like the * amount indicated in the extravagant statement of my hon. friend. He said we could buy rails in the United States if we paid for them. I say it can not be done; we have tried it. Nor can we buy rails in Canada unless we take the steel companies off the manufacturing of billets to make shells with; and it is necessary, by Heavens, to keep these going in order to win the war. It don't make any difference; anything they want for the war they. will get it, no matter what it is.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I congratulate the House, and I congratulate the Government, upon the very admirable speech the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) has made. It is a delight to this side of the House to have the minister unbosom himself, to take the House into his confidence and let us really know what he has in his mind with regard to this matter.
The minister has done, I think, the very best he could, but in the end he tells us that he is going to look after Edson although he does not know how he he is going to do it. I wou,ld like to ask the House if it would not have been better for the minister to have asked for a day or two's delay before finally disposing of this matter so that he could have informed the House-[DOT]

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Of course, nothing can be delayed on that side.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
The minister says that
he is going to tear up all the rails in Canada in order to win the war.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
No, I did not say
that.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: If necessary to win the war. That is a very laudable desire and I think we would all agree to it if it were necessary to win the war. We would do anything that could be done, but the -question is. whether the minister has done the wisest thing that he could have done having that object in view. What is the excuse that the minister gives? Here we have a condition in the West where the line which is being stripped of its rails is a part of the main transcontinental railway connecting the Atlantic with the Pacific and a railway which was built for the purpose of carrying on transcontinental business. It has been explained by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that for a considerable distance in the section of the mountains where these rails are to be taken up, the Canadian Northern runs along one side of a lake, some 30 miles in length, and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other side, and that there is a large colliery to which accommodation is being, given whose development has been created by the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not care how many engineers the minister gets out there, unless he can replace these nails on that portion of the line which runs past the Jasper collieries, he cannot give accommodation to them. It is absolutely clear from the statement which has -been made by my hon. friend from Edmonton that unless the track is re-laid he would have to build a bridge three miles long across the lake in order to connect the Jaspar colleries with the Canadian Northern railway, .so that St would be necessary that the rails which he is having taken up from this portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific shall be supplied by rails from some other source in order to give the accommodation that he says he is going to give. Just how he is going to give it he does not know. I think it is very unfortunate that the minister did not learn from his engineers how this accommodation could be given to the town of Edson, the Jasper collieries and all that section of the country before deciding to take this drastic measure of stripping this railway of its rails. The minister says that the British Government wanted these rails. These rails, I suppose, weigh 90 pounds to the yard. The minister will correct me if I am wrong.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Eighty pounds.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: There are many portions of the Government railway system where the rails are very much lighter.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Have they the same borings?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by borings?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Do you not know? Then, if you do not, you ought not to talk about it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I do not know; I am ignorant upon the subject. What is the meaning of it?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Different railways have rails with different borings. The rails of the Canadian Pacific are not bored in the same way. as the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific, or of the Canadian Northern. They particularly asked us to send rails of the same borings so that there would be no trouble in making the connections.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: That strikes me as a most absurd statement. Do I understand by borings that the minister means the rolling of the rails, or does he mean the boltings?-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: For making the connections? That is what I thought it was. Can the minister explain to you, Mr. Speaker, how, if 20, or 30, or 40, or 50, or 100 miles of rails were sent over there to be laid, it would make much difference as to what the borings were upon that 100 miles?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Well, the British Government do not know what they want, of course, according to the hon. gentleman'.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
We heard the other day that the British engineers thought it would take six weeks to lay some few miles of railway track, but Jack Stewart, a Canadian, and his fellow officers did the business in four days. I am not disposed to place the judgment of British engineers above that of Canadian engineers.
M/. COCHRANE:	They are Canadian
engineers who- are laying the railway.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Surely, if there were 50 miles of rails taken from a portion of the Grand Trunk Pacific system, and weighing 80 pounds to the yard, and if there were 50 miles of other rails, all they would have to do would toe to make one connection and the rest of the laying would be uniform. There is hardly a railway in Canada on which you will not see two or more classes of rails. You will see old rails, some 60,

some 65 and some 70 pounds to the yard, and you will see new rails weighing 80 pounds to the yard, and in some cases 90 pounds. I am reminded by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) that some rails from Ithe Canadian Northern railway are being placed on the Transcontinental railway and there is no reason in the world why it should not be done. I know that they have laid new rails on the Intercolonial railway and that there are many miles of the road where for years there was a different description of rail, a different weight of rail and a rail having different borings used from that which was used on other portions of the line. Men acquainted with the practical work of laying rails have no difficulty, and it is all moonshine for the minister to tell me, and to tell this House, that the British Government, or the engineers of the British Government, require that the rails should be . of the same weight and of the same borings. It is too absurd and every man in this House knows it. It is not necessary to be Minister of Railways to know that. Any member of this House who knows anything about railways at all will know that the statement I make is absolutely correct. We have had it in our own experience and it is within the knowledge of every man who has lived alongside of a line of railway. I have heard it stated by gentlemen who have been at the front that what is required in France is rails for the building of light railways. I think they are narrow gauge railways a3 a rule. That is what I have been told. I have not had the opportunity -and a very great opportunity it would have been-of being at the front, but I have been informed by gentlemen who have been there that the railways are light railways and usually narrow gauge. Of course, necessarily, they are carrying comparatively light loads and a light rail would be all that would be required. I think the minister would have been better advised if he had taken rails weighing 60 or 65 pounds to the yard, which could have been got from many of the railways in Eastern Canada, and sent them to the front. But the minister, apparently without touching the Canadian Pacific, without touching the Canadian Northern, without touching the rails which are lying at Hudson Bay for the Hudson Bay railway, goes to the railway which this Government would like to discredit. I say that advisedly notwithstanding that the minister may deny it. This Government started in when the rail-
way was nearly built to discredit it by changing the grades or rather by not making the grades up to the specification and not making the railway the first-class road which the late Government intended it should be. They have not provided proper terminals in connection with it. They have neglected altogether the national obligation which rested upon them insofar as Eastern Canada was concerned to create terminals for the Grand Trunk Pacific upon the St. Lawrence at Quebec and at St. John which was to be the eastern freight terminus of the Transcontinental railway. They have absolutely neglected their duty in that respect. They did not create the terminals at Quebec which they were to do. They made, at great expense, a change which will take away very largely from the usefulness of the Grand Trunk Pacific as a transcontinental gnad. They have done all this without the consent of the authorities of 'the 'Grand Trunk Pacific, and no-w they go to work, as a final step in the wrecking of a national railway, and take up the rails Which are owned by the bondholders of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, because, if the company is in default, these (bondholders have a right to look to the railway, to its equipment, to its rails, to its entire property, as their security. The Government have done that without even saying " by your leave " to these bondholders, who are the ones immediately interested., not merely the first bondholders, whose bonds are guaranteed by the Government, but any second or third bondholders who may have liens against the road. They have no right to do that without the consent of these gentlemen. Therefore, I for one feel bound to say that, notwithstanding the statement of the Minister of Railways, he could have done much more effective service for the British Government in getting rails in eastern Canada where it would not have been necessary to make this break in a great transcontinental .system; he would have been, able to do it with less expense, and with much less likelihood of the British Government being called upon to pay heavy damages.
I think also it is to be regretted that the minister simply tells ns to-day that he is going to look after this colliery and is going to look after Edson, but does not say how. There is another serious phase to this question. The interruption at this time of the operation of a great coal mine in western Canada is a matter of the most serious character.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Will the interruption of the operation of that coal mine or the interruption of the prosecution of the war at the front toe the more serious matter for Canada?
iMr. PUGSLEY: I should like to see both carried on. I should like to see no interruption of the collieries operation, and no interruption of the war.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
You do not speak
like it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: But I think the interest of the people of Canada ought to be considered also. This Government does not seem to care one iota for the people of Canada.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: They think they can get great glory and kudos because our boys go to the front and perform heroic deeds. They think they can get great kudos by sending rails to England. They think they can get great kudos by lending money to the Imperial Munitions Board to build ships in Canada. But they have taken no single step, so far, for the benefit of the people of Canada. They have taken no step to improve transportation.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Does the hon. member not consider that the Canadian boys at the front, whose condition is going to be alleviated by the construction of railroads, are part of the people of Canada?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I certainly do, but I consider that there are people left in Canada too. We have to-day the spectacle of the interests of the people of Canada being entirely neglected by this Government. Let me give a few instances while I am' on my feet. 1 do this because the Minister of Railways has spoken as he has done. Look at the cost of coal. I speak of this because keeping down the price of coal and supplying coal to our people in abundance is of great importance both in the East and in the West, and any interruption of a great coal mining industry in the West must prove a very great disadvantage. We have learned that several collieries in western Canada are closed. There is very great danger of people being short of fuel, and to be short of fuel in our Canadian West when the winter season comes on might almost bring the people to a state when many of them might freeze to death. Is that of no concern to. the minister?
Apparently not. Apparently he has not thought of that question at all; he tears up these rails, which are necessary in order to give that colliery an outlet for their product. So in regard to shipbuilding, if the Minister of Marine will allow me to say a word upon it. I do it because it is a question-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member must confine himself to the subject under discussion.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I am referring to this because the Minister of Railways has made a charge against me, and has said that he would do everything in order to win the war.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways has no authority to vary the rules of the House.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The Minister of Railways interrupts the House so seldom that, perhaps, great privileges should be given to him when he does, and I might be pardoned for following him; hut, Sir, I bow to your ruling cheerfully. I say to the minister as a last word, in all sincerity, that he can get an abundance of rails in eastern Canada without interfering with the operation of a transcontinental system. He can get them without interfering with any great industry. He ought to do that, and the fact that he has not disturbed the Canadian Northern railway or the Canadian Pacific railway-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I am disturbing the Canadian Northern railway, and the hon. member admitted that we were disturbing it.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Where?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: We are replacing the Grand Trunk Pacific rails with Canadian Northern rails.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: But the minister is not taking up any rails from the Canadian Northern railway to send abroad.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
He is not doing that. He merely lays hold of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and that is evidence that he has but very little regard as to whether or not he interrupts the business of a transcontinental railway. To stop a great railway like the Grand Trunk Pacific while it is being stripped of its rails means a very great deal of damage which somebody will



have to pay in the future. The taking up of the rails without the consent of the bondholders is also a matter of very great importance. Will the minister allow me to ask him to submit to this House, if he will, the correspondence which he has had with regard to the furnishing of rails, and also any correspondence or agreement which he has had with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company with respect to the taking up of these rails. I should be very glad if the minister would do that.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, like the hon. gentleman from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), reside in the province of Alberta. I have received telegrams and letters asking me to investigate the circumstances under which the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway are being lifted west of Edmonton. I have contented myself with making the most careful investigation possible, and I do not propose tc enter into any discussion in this House this afternoon as to the past railroad history in this country. I shall tell the House shortly the story as I have obtained it after the most careful investigation. The authorities overseas requested the Dominion of Canada to furnish 300 miles of rails of a given weight. Thev asked at the same time that the abnormal number of 1,200 turnouts be supplied with the 300 miles of track. Any gentleman who is familiar with railroad matters knows that 1,200 turn-outs is out of all proportion to 300 miles of track. It is, as you will observe, four turnouts to the mile. I ascertained further, not only from what I have seen, but from what I have been told by engineers, that these rails were required to be of great weight, and the turn-outs of equal weight, because the rails are being laid at night under shell fire; they are being laid for a given, definite purpose, and that purpose is to enable us to fight the enemy with heavy artillery rather than with flesh and blood as we have done on previous occasions. These rails it is necessary to lay "to save the lives of Canadian soldiers in France and Flanders. Those are facts that cannot possibly be controverted. You ask me why the abnormal number of four turnouts to the mile are required, and I have to say to you only this: I have been told by engineers of eminence now in France who have come here and gone back that a heavy rail is necessary properly to anchor the heavy artillery at a given point to shell the enemy. The heavy artillery requires the heaviest pos-

sible kind of rail, and those rails necessarily require the heavy turnouts, which, as hon. gentlemen know, are merely little break-ings-off or turnings-out from the main line. Four turnouts to the mile are required in order that our gallant railway construction corps in France-working under conditions such as men have never worked under be-, fore; at night, with very little light, the shells of the enemy falling everywhere about them-may be able to provide for the proper anchoring of guns that weigh eighty tons and for the sending within the next hour of shells into the enemy's lines. In view of these facts, I am sure the House will have an adequate^appreciation of why we were asked for 300 miles of rails and 1,200 turnouts.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
By turnouts, does the
hon. gentleman mean what we call sidings?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Not sidings. Sometimes they are called sidings in this country, but I have called them turnouts or ' switches. From the line extending towards the German front a short line of rail is laid-sometimes a quarter of a mile in length; sometimes half a mile. Heavy rails and adequate turnouts are nectessary in order that the cars upon which are mounted guns weighing in some cases as much as eighty tons may be firmly held and shells weighing sometimes a ton may be sent toward the German lines. It is hardly necessary for me to say- that the concussion-the kick, as we called it when we were boys-is very great, and that, consequently, the use of very heavy steel and the exercise of great care are necessary.
When we were asked for 300 miles of rails and 1,200 turnouts, what did we do? The Government of Canada, an integral part of the warring powers, a unit on the side of the Allies, replied: to the extent of our ability, we wiill supply these rails and turnouts. The Government did not go to the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific, or the Canadian Northern. They went to the National Transcontinental railway, the property of the people of Canada, because it iwais felt, having regard to other means of communication, that the removal of rails from that line would cause the least disturbance to traffic and would be a representative loan from all the Canadian people of steel rails for this purpose. So, at various terminals and at isiwitches and .sidings, 300 miles of rails and 1,200 turnouts were taken up. These 1,200 turnouts were not all taken from the National Transcontinental; some

were acquired by purchase; some were taken from other portions of the Canadian roads. Let me explain where the difficulty comes in. A turnout is bored with regard to the rail that is used on the line. If, it was merely a matter oif laying a straight line and using 50, 60, 70, 90 or 100 pound rails, there would be no .difficulty. When I went West the Canadian Pacific Railway was laid with 56 pound rails. On some portions of the New York Central between Ottawa and New York, 90 and 112 pound rails are uped. If the line is a straight one, you can use different weights of rail as you proceed, but if the line is not straight, the turnouts are bored to match the particular kind of rail used. The rail of the weight and boring used omi our lines and the turnout adopted thereto, were those that this Government, in response to the request of our Allies, .procured by taking up portions of the National Trancontinental and by purchase.
It is quite true, as the member for Edmonton has said, that all of these rails are not in France. Would to God they were! We should all be glad if they were-.but they are not. The German submarine is upon the high seas; transport is becoming very difficult. We have not been able to ship all those rails to France, but, to the extent of the ability of the merchant marine of England and France to carry them, these rails have been .shipped to France and some of them that were taken from the Transcontinental line, together with the turnouts that were provided, are to-dtay making it passible for our artillery to hurl shells into the German lines.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will give us the information that the Minister of Railways refused to give, and will tell us how many rails have gone to France.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: It has been thought advisable in war that those charged with high responsibility should not disclose all they know. I do not pretend to know how many miles of rails have been sent or how many have reached France. All I know is that some have reached France, and I am sure, knowing the hon. memlber for Edmonton as I do, that he, for one, will rejoice that that is a fact.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The old story-the censorship to protect incompetence and ignorance.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Then it has been largely in use by my hon. friend during the most of
his life. In the light of those facts, concerning which there need be no controversy, I am sure that many a gentleman on the other side of the House is proud that we have been able to supply the rails. I do not think that we should have any acrimonious contention concerning matters of this kind. Why should we? If I read aright the countenances of hon. .gentlemen opposite, I do not think they are rejoicing in the fact that we .had to talse up rails. I feel that they, like myself, deprecate the fact that we are in the midst of a great war. But I am sure most of them believe, as I do, that the welfare of this State and our civilization are threatened. If, therefore, we can do this little bit to save our boys at the front and make it possible for them to become more effective, why in the name of Heaven should we not do it? Why in the name of Heaven should we not rejoice in doing it? Does any man. in this . House believe that we should not do it?
Having supplied 300 miles of rails and 1,200 turnouts, we were asked for further quantities of the same kind of rail and turnout. There was just one source from which that class of rail with the particular bore required could be obtained, and that was on the Grand Trunk Pacific. There were some, it is true, on the Hudson Bay railway, but they had not the adequate turnouts. So we went West. I was interested in this matter because I received telegrams from gentlemen asking me to look into it. The minister, unlike some of my hon. friends, did not arrogate- to himself a knowledge which he said he did not possess. He said: I leave this matter to engineers who know much more than I. He said to them: Gentlemen, I want you to go West; I want you, undqr the direction of the Chief Railway Commissioner of Canada, who has knowledge of the traffic conditions, to determine how we can best serve our people overseas and at the same time do the least injury to traffic conditions in Canada. The judgment of engineers such as those who dealt with this matter is entitled to much consideration. They went to the Grand Trunk Pacific and they looked the situation over. They found that they could take up the rails to which my hon. friend has referred, and that 600 additional turnouts could be Obtained, making a total of 1,800 turnouts, or switches, and 600 miles of track. And what happened? The rails on the Grand Trunk Pacific are being taken up. Rails are being torn up from the Canadian Northern grades and shifted over to

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is exceeding the rules of debate.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I am asking the question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: It is not in order for the hon. member to say, by indirect methods, what he cannot say directly.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend knows a little better than to say what he has said.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I will put it in this way. Can anything be more tragic than that any member of this House should speak about the rights of bondholders, when the British Government and the Canadian Government have put the collective credit and weight of the resources of the British Empire behind 300 miles of track? That is really what this means. In the midst of a great struggle, we have on the one hand a few bondholders interested in 300 miles of track, and on the other, the combined

resources of the British Empire to make good the damages, the making good of which is guaranteed by this Dominion, and by the obligations, not only of Great Britain, but of France. Such a condition of affairs simply beggars description. I cannot keep myself within the rules of order and adequately describe it.
Mr. PiUGSLEY: Then the hon. member had better sit down.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I have no doubt my hon. friend would like me to do so.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
No, I like to see the hon.
member on his feet.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Nothing more remains to be said in relation to the question except one observation in regard to the collieries. The collieries have not been put out of business; it is not proposed to put them out of business, and it has not been suggested that they will be put out of business. The cold facts are that the lay-out has been arranged so that the collieries may continue to be served, and, as I have said, my assurance is that unless that could be done the rails would not be moved. I still think that the rights of the citizens of Alberta can be protected without any violent attack being made against individuals, who, at tht moment, happen to occupy a place of responsibility under the Crown. I still believe that the interests of the Dominion of Canada are, at this moment, so inextricably involved with those of Great Britain and France that any service that we can render, however small or insignificant it may apparently be, involving merely the moving of a few miles of rails and a few hundred turnouts, should be done so gladly, so willingly, that in no Parliament that I can conceive of within the Empire would a thoughtful, responsible member of Parliament take up the time that might well be otherwise used in finding fault with the patriotic and willing service that is being rendered by the Government that happens, for the time being, to be placed in the position where it can respond to the reasonable demands that are made upon it by those who are directing military operations overseas?
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) : Mr. Speaker, the words of the chief of the National Service Board strike us with a great lack of harmony. He chastises members of the House for wasting its time in useless talk, but a good portion of his time was taken up in backing in and out of the rules of order of the House. He could not, in this time of stress, keep within the
rules of debate, in referring to an hon. member on this side of the House who dared to discuss this question. As a member of this House, I am becoming heartily sick of the way in which every time a member on this side discusses any question, some hon. member on the opposite side challenges his loyalty, directly or indirectly.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: Disgusting.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend, the Chief of the National Service Board-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: What board is that?

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
The late lamented
National Service Board. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) has no right to lecture us on what is being done in connection with this war. We understand our responsibilities, and we are not going to he frightened from exercising our Tights even by the imperious manner of the hon. member for Calgary. He says that we are all interested in the war. So we are, and for my part whatever is best for winning the war I am prepared to support. That is my way of thinking, but there is one thing that is not in the interest of this war, and that is the giving of lectures like the one to which we have just listened.	'
We should not boast of what we have done to win the war, for .none of us has done too much, and none of us can do too much. I was particularly pained at a reference of the Minister of Railways to my hon. friend for Edmonton, for if there is a man in Canada who has done his duty in this war it is my hon. friend who sits to my left (Mr. Oliver). He is represented today by a living presence in the trenches, and he is also represented in a grave in France, and when he rises to discuss a question of this kind he does so because he feels It is in the interests of the people he represents. He has a perfect right to do so, and if sacrifice be the measure of that right he has the right to as full an extent as any man in Canada. We are not helping the cause by flinging these aspersions across the floor of the House about disloy alty. I take it for granted that the heart of the people of Canada beats true to the great cause in which we are engaged, and so long as we are actuated by that spirit let us talk like reasonable men, and not criticise each other as if disloyalty lurked in the breast of any one. The Canadian people are true to this great cause. However we may differ on other things, we stand united for the winning of the war, and we

will not rest until that purpose has been accomplished.
Now what is this question over which the Government and the sub-Government have lest their temper? It is as to whether the rails should have been taken up in one particular part of Canada and from one particular railway. No hon. gentleman has suggested for a moment, and I should be ashamed of him if he did, that we should not hasten to comply with the request of the British Government for rails that were necessary to the winning of the war. The question of bringing up the heavy artillery is one we do not understand so well as those who have been to the front, but we are told that it is of vital importance, and 1 am sure that the history of the war during the last few weeks must have convinced us beyond all cavil, that a great deal of our success depends upon the use of heavy artillery. We all want to do our share, but are we doing it in the right way? I am not going to criticise the Minister of Railways unfairly, but this fact does undoubtedly stand out: the people of Canada are suspicious, and with some cause, that this Government has never attempted to make a success of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, and when the minister at first blush and without consultation, so far as we know, rushed to that system for the rails that were required, the people began to suspect that that was tantamount to saying the system was no good. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) says that the rails were of little, use because the road had carried practically no war supplies, and that is one thing I am going to charge against the Government when the proper time comes. Having a railway of our own to carry supplies, running through Canadian territory from the Pacific to the Atlantic, the Government refused to use the road for the transport of supplies for the front, but gave the traffic to the other lines. The hon member for Calgary has told me in advance that I am right in that regard.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend followed me. I said that the sections which were affected by the tearing up of these rails were not carrying supplies for the front or munitions of war. I think there are three passenger trains running.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I admit one thing, that I am following my hon. friend. He again admits that this traffic in war supplies was given to other lines. When the Government were asked for rails, they went at once tr
flVIr. Graham.)
the Transcontinental. Now if, as they intimate, that road was of little use before, they made it of still less use by taking up the sidings. I am not going to say that the Government did wrong; I want to be fait in my criticism, and I would criticise nothing that I thought made for efficiency in the winning of the war. But the long railway address of my hon. friend from Calgary as to the turnouts did not impress me. He says that the Transcontinental sidings did not have the number of turnouts to the mile that were necessary. My hon. friend is right as to the turnout itself, but you can take any rail and have a turnout to fit that rail. The moment the turnout is made, rails of any quality of steel or weight can be adjusted, the only change involved being at one joint.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: They asked for these rails.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: My hon. friend's argument as to turnouts was therefore no argument at all, so far as railway construction is concerned. His next point was that the British Government asked for rails with the same boring. I am not going to quarrel with that statement, though as a humble citizen I might be allowed to say that the fact of the British Government asking for a particular thing is not absolute proof that it is the proper thing to do under the circumstances, because they have changed their mind on several matters. It is therefore not a sine qua non that it is always right to leave it to the British Government. Why did they ask for these rails? It was for one of two reasons: either they were easier of construction and could be laid more quickly and with greater safety under fire. Now, I have not heard any one say there is any great difference between the time consumed in laying the Grand Trunk Pacific rails and rails of another pattern. The borings and the fishplates are of a different style.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: The bolts are different.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: A different boring would include a different bolt, of course.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: By using these rails there was less liability of a mix-up.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I know the two styles of rails pretty well and I have not been told by any one that there is any great difference in the time it takes to lay them. . If General Stewart tells me that he can lay these rails more quickly and with greater safety under fire than rails of the other

kind, I will say at once that these rails ought to be sent, but I do not take any stock myself in that argument.
As to the paralleling of tracks, the hon. member for Calgary points out that the colliery is going to be looked after, and he chastised us severely for suggesting that we should look after the coal mine in preference to the war. My hon. friend shakes his head; somebody said that, and I think it was the minister. At all events the hon. member for Calgary admits that he looked after the coal mine first, and after that, he did the patriotic thing.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I do not know
anything about the colliery except that I received a telegram from some one interested in it. I have no interest in it myself of any kind.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
I was not suggesting that my hon. friend was financially interested in it. But he first investigated as to whether this colliery of has friends would he injured or not, and, finding that it would not be injured-" A'll right, take up the rails." But here is the position:	If the
colliery on one side of the lake is to be looked after by taking up the Canadian Northern rails and placing them where the Grand Trunk Pacific rails are now, the colliery on the other side will be robbed of its transportation facilities. You cannot serve the two. I have been on that ground, and I know.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
My information
i>s that all the collieries will be looked after.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
Then it can only he by
taking up the rails and laying them down again in the same place. I have been on that ground within a month and a half, and I say that if the rails are taken from the Grand 'Trunk Pacific on one side of the lake, and replaced by rails taken from the Canadian Northern on the other side of the lake, the collieries on the side now being served by the Canadian Northern will have no transportation facilities. You cannot have the rails and not have them at the same time. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is interested

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
But I tell him that
in a day or two I will have a map here-

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext: But you can't draw coal on a map.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
You can draw rails
on a map.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC RAILWAY. REMOVAL, OF RAILS FOR USE IN FRANCE.
speechtext:
The question has been
raised why these collieries should .object, as they are not going to be injured. But the hon. member for Edmonton has telegram after telegram to the effect tlhat they are going to be injured. It is his duty, then, to raise the question. He would he doing less than his duty if he did not urge the minister to the fullest extent of his power to see if it is not possible, without interfering with the efficiency of carrying on the war, to avoid impairing the industries of the western country, particularly those engaged in the production of coal.
And now, let me say this as my closing word: Let us discuss these questions with one single eye to the winning of the war- that is the first thing, of course. But when an hon. member on this side of the House, who has done what the hon. member for Edmonton has done, raises such a question as has been raised here to-day, it ill becomes any member to insinuate that he is impelled or inspired by any other than the highest
5 p.m. motives. We want to accomplish what is before us, hut we shall never accomplish it if we distrust one another in the matter of loyalty. We have our own ideas, and to these ideas w^ hold strongly; hut for Heaven's sake, in discussing these matters upon which we are supposed to be united, let us stop accusing one another, on trifling provocation, of not showing as much loyalty on one side of this House as on the other.
Motion negatived.

Civil Government-Department of Trade and Commerce, Salaries, $133,700.

Will the minister give
us some information as to the Commissioner of Trade and Commerce whose salary is provided for in this Estimate. I do not know that any statement that has been made in the House as to this gentleman. Who is he, how long has he been in the service, and what are his duties?

First let me say with regard to this, item that there is no increase in the number of officials; the increase in the amount asked for as compared with last year is due wholly to the regular statutory increases. It will be remembered that Mt. Richard Grigg, who was Commissioner of Trade and Commerce, died very

suddenly about a year and a half ago. His loss, of course was very much felt by the department. Under the confused conditions of trade and commerce I have not felt in a position to make a new appointment, and am not quite sure whether I shall fill the position with an officer performing exactly the same duties as Mr. Grigg performed. But there will he an appointment of a man of superior class who will take over perhaps more extended and slightly different duties, in view of the reconstruction period that is upon us,

Does the minister think it tends to the smooth working of a department to put men under the deputy minister with higher salaries than that paid to the deputy, who is the operating head of the department? I know that this has been the practice in some cases under the late Government, as well as under their present succesisors, 'but it always seemed to me a mistake.

It does not seem to be fair that you should pin down the department, no matter what its possibilities or necessities were in the light of the service required, or that if you find a technical, or scientific, officer, some one who is required for a very special purpose, you shall be debarred from getting his services simply because you do not want to exceed the salary which is given for a deputy minister. If you took that position and made a hard and fast rule you would bar the possibility of securing the best service in certain particulars.

I would like to make a proposition to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. I will not exact an answer to-day, but I will make the proposition. I have a Bill before the House, No. 22, which 'affects the minister's department in connection with the indemnity to be granted to workmen who are injured while in the employ of the Government in terminal elevators in the West. The minister is familiar with that question. Unfortunately, labourers or employees of any kind, who are in the employ of the Government in the elevators at Moosejaw, Saskatoon, or other places, on being injured, have no claim under the Workmen's Compensation Act. Employees of His Majesty should not be in an inferior position to that of employees in any other elevator. This matter has already been the subject of discussion. I doubt if my Bill will be reached. We have allowed the minister's estimates to go through pretty easily, and perhaps he will tell us if he
CSir George Foster.]
would take the matter into consideration so that we might have the Bill discussed this session.
I have not really seen my hon. friend's Bill yet. Has the Bill been printed?
Yes.
I have not looked into it, but I will be very glad to do so and let my hon. friend know.

Some time ago I asked the minister if it was his intention to introduce a Bill to amend the Manitoba Grain Act, and my hon. friend told me that he expected to. I have been waiting for the introduction of the Bill. I wish to propose some amendments to .the Manitoba Grain Act. I would like to have an assurance from my hon. friend that he is going to bring in a Bill to amend the Act; otherwise, I shall have to bring in a Bill myself to amend it and I would rather not do that.

I am afraid that I cannot give my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff ) any more definite information than I did before and that was that I did expect to bring in a Bill. I am having very closely canvassed now certain representations that have been made in reference to the amendment of the Act. I may say with reference to amendments that the number proposed has been legion but not very many have survived the investigation that has been put upon them and these are not at present being pressed, but there are some three or four that I have had called to my attention and which are now receiving the consideration of the Grain Board. As soon as I receive the report from them I will be able to indicate what the proposed amendments are, if any. If it is possible at all to do without amending the Act this year I should be very glad.
When my hon. friend was discussing the Estimates, did he state to the committee who had been appointed to succeed the late Mr. Grigg.

No appointment.

Maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and ice breakers, $1,180,000.
The amount asked is the same as last year. The expenditure in 1915-16 was $1,124,708.21 and in 1916-17 we kept the expenditure down to $962,048.48. We are asking for the same appropriation as last year, although I hope to be able to keep the expenditure below the appropriation by nearly $200,000.
Does the minister not think that he might set a good example by reducing the Estimates to the actual amount that he thinks he will spend?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The officials of the depart->ment, those who are at the head of the different branches and charged very largely with the responsibility, subject, of course, to the minister's responsibility, do not like the Estimates to be cut down to the last dollar. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Have you the same number of icebreakers as you had three or four years ago?	'

speechtext:
The Earl Grey and the

Of course, we expect that by next winter the service formerly rendered by these steamers will be performed by the car ferry, as the piers on each side of the strait are nearing completion. icebreaking operations on the St. Lawrence this year satisfactory?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That varies with the number of wrecks. The year before last, the cost was $12,241, and last year, $4,807. It will be rather gratifying to the House to know that last year, for the first time in 63 years, there was not a casualty between Quebec and Father Point. The wreck commissioner is Captain Demers, a permanent official of the department and a member of the Civil Service. We have also a wreck commissioner on the Pacific coast who receives $1,500. It was found that to have Captain Demers go to the Pacific coast every time there was a wreck there involved great loss of time and also a good deal of expense.

I think that Captain Demers is a very satisfactory officer indeed, and, so far as I know, he discharges his duties fearlessly and impartially. The custom of having assessors in inquiries is a long and well-established one. I think, however, that the chief examiner, in this case, Mr. Demers, should have absolute and full authority to select his own assessors. In Halifax, where many inquiries take place, it has become the practice of members of political patronage committees to insist upon the appointment of the assessors.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have no business to.

I think that political patronage should be absolutely eliminated in matters of this kind. A better practice would be to allow the examiner to select his own assessor; no outside persons at

points where inquiries are instituted should be consulted as to assistants or asked to recommend them. I know of one or two' instances where men who were not qualified were appointed assessors. I am glad that the minister does not approve of that practice; I hope that he will do everything in His power to prevent its recurrence. The investigation of wrecks is a very important matter. The responsibility of the chief commissioner is very great; the future of captains and officers of the ships involved in any disaster .is at stake. The commissioner should have the assistance' of strong, independent and impartial men; he, therefore, would be the better person to select his assessors.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I entirely concur in what my hon. friend has said. The wreck commissioner's court should be entirely free from any political interference. My attention was directed, within the last year or so, to the fact that in certain places suggestions were being made to the wreck commissioner that certain persons should be appointed. I at once gave instructions to my deputy that the wreck commissioner dhould exercise his own judgment in every case; that he should appoint men whom he thought qualified to act as assessors.
That should be communicated to the wreck commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It has been communicated to him. When Mr. Demers is called, say, to some part of the Maritime Provinces to hold an inquiry, orders are issued, signed by myself, for the holding of the inquiry and for the appointment of assessors, the latter in blank. Mr. Demers, when he reaches the place of investigation, selects the best men he can find to act as assessors, and fills in the names on the order for the appointment of assessors. There is absolutely no interference with the authority of the wreck commissioner in regard to the matter. .
Ocean and river service-Expenses of schools of navigation, $3,000.
Will the minister state what is being done in connection with the schools of navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no change in the estimate from that of previous years. The amount spent last year up to March 31 under this head was $4,461, and in the previous year $4,067. The item is to cover all expenditures in connection with the de-

partment's free navigation schools for the fiscal year 1917-18. Free navigation schools are now in operation as follows: For the whole year, at Halifax, N.S., Captain John Simmons, instructor, $80 a month, and at St. John, N.B., Captain R. C. Cole, $75 a month. For the winter months only, at Quebec, P.Q., Captain P. L. Lachance, instructor, $600 per annum; North Sydney, N.S., Captain James Sutherland, $250 per season; Yarmouth, N.S., Captain J. E. Murphy, $250 per season; Charlottetown, P.E.I., Captain James Lumsdane, $75 a month; Collingwood, Ont., Captain George C. Coles, $250 a season; Kingston, Ont., Captain Steeves, paid by Queen's University; Vancouver, B.C. , Captain Charles Eddie, salary covered by yearly salary as examiner of masters and mate3. We pay Queen's University $500 for the season. The university employs a competent professor, gives free instruction, provides class rooms, and pays all expenses. At Vancouver, Captain Charles Eddie receives no salary as instructor, his remuneration being covered by the yearly salary paid him as examiner of masters and mates. The school at Charlottetown is a new school, opened in December last. There was a very general demand for a school in Prince Edward Island, which has turned out a great many sailors.
Was the school there a success?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Last year three certificates were granted to masters of coasting vessels, four to mates of coasting vessels, and one to a master of inland and minor waters. Not many certificates were granted, but, perhaps, better results will 'be obtained when the school has been longer in operation. If not, we shall have to consider the desirability of continuing the school. At the suggestion of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), a school of navigation was established at Baie des Chaleurs, and the work was attended with some degree of success. Unfortunately, however, the gentleman who had been conducting it went away and we could not get any one else in the community who had the necessary knowledge to continue the school.
Would the hon. gentleman continue it this year if an1 instructor to carry on the work were obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the results of the experiment justified it, certainly we should be prepared to continue the school.

The minister referred
to the fact that in Vancouver one gentleman acts as examiner of mates and instructor in the school of navigation. I think that that would not be a good system to follow definitely.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite right. That is the only case of the kind. I do not think it is desirable that the practice should 'Continue, and we are making arrangements to discontinue it.

I regret that the minister has not taken this matter up with a little more vigour.
