The matter of enabling our young imen to secure navigation licenses not only in 'Halifax and Charlottetown, but in the towns on the coast of the Maritime Provinces, on the Great Lakes and on the Pacific, !is a matter of considerable importance. The question of doing something in connection with the technical school at Halifax was brought to my hon. friend's attention on several occasions, but he does not seem to have made any progress in that regard. We have an excellent technical school in Halifax and we have branches in various parts of the province where men qualify themselves in the coal mining and steel industries. In the town in which I live a large number of young boyis, many of them apprentices in the steel works, receive training at nights in the technical schools which are affiliated with the Provincial Technical School at Halifax. There is no reason why in the larger Maritime coast towns some system should not be established by which the young men should learn to build boats, handle and repair gasolene engines and obtain navigation licenses.
This question of technical education is, of course, a big one; but so far as the maritime industries of this country are con-eernfecf, I think it could be developed by my hon. friend without very much expense. It is absurd to think that we are spending in the whole of Canada only $4,000 a year in educating our young men for maritime service. The fact is that they have to pick up their education elsewhere as it is not provided by the Government, and even in the city of Halifax where there is a school of navigation, there are private enterprises receiving no assistance from the Government where men are training boys to pass marine examinations. The same thing is occurring in other places throughout the country, so that what we are doing is not effective, and I wish the minister would take the matter up in a

bigger way and, either in conjunction with the technical schools or otherwise, would give the young men in the towns along the coast an opportunity of receiving lessons in marine matters. That would be a great advantage to the country, because if we are going to build up a mercantile marine we must have sailors and officers. No later than to-day I received a letter from a gentleman in the province of Ontario stating that it was impossible for him to secure officers for an ocean-going ship. Officers are scarce; they are more difficult to secure now, I suppose, than they ever were before, so that we should be doing something in the way of training officers, and if the minister could think of any scheme whereby this opportunity would be given to young men of Canso, Shelburne, Liverpool, Lunenburg and other places that I might mention on the coast of the Maritime Provinces, it would be of great advantage to the young men of those localities and would enable them to get so far ahead with their studies that they could pass the examinations without going to Halifax or Charlottetown or any of those places to attend school. It is out of the question for a large number of those men who are not wealthy to go away from home in order to attend school at Halifax or any of those other places, and education of that kind should be brought to their doors by some method. That is the question with which I would like my hon. friend to deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In regard to what my hon. friend said in the first instance, I may say that at Halifax this work is going on in conjunction with the technical school. Mr. Simmons there is employed with the approval of the officers of the technical school, and the work is done in the technical college itself, so that we are in harmony with them and co-operating with them in regard to this matter.
My hon. friend says that there should be some general policy in regard to technical education. There is a certain constitutional difficulty in this country in regard to technical education. Education is, of course, assigned, under the British North America Act, to the provinces, and there is no doubt that there are certain provinces of Canada which are very jealous of their rights, and when communications were addressed to them on the subject by a previous Government, they gave their views with regard to the matter and were not prepared to say whether they would favour a Federal

Government coming into the field of technical education. I think, however, that is a matter that should be disposed of, if possible, by mutual compromise, and I hope some day to see this country embarking on a large scale on a scheme of technical education, because I believe it would be of enormous advantage to the country from many standpoints, and I do not think any . country can become great industrially unless it has a proper system of technical education. I think, however, a great deal of that work can be done by the provincial schools. The technical school at Halifax is a step forward in the right direction, and I understand there is at Toronto a school that is maintained by the city or municipality, and that is also a step forward. But the time will come when the question will have to be dealt with in a large way, and there will have to be a very large expenditure made in regard to it. I do not think it is desirable to have small technical schools scattered here and there throughout the country, but some broad policy will have to be adopted in the future. There has already been a good deal of discussion in this country in regard to this question, and a commission which was appointed' has sent in a very interesting report. I refer to the commission of which Mr. James Robertson was the chairman.
I have no doubt if conditions were normal, that report would have been considered and probably the question would have been dealt with, but at present, of course, it is not easy to consider such large expenditures as would be necessary in order to deal with the question in a broad manner.
Is the minister satisfied that nothing could be done through the technical school at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The technical school at Halifax, from what I am told, is a very excellent institution, and perhaps something could be done; but it is a school,
I understand, absolutely controlled by the provincial government, and as I have stated, under the British North America Act, the local Governments are charged with the duty of education. In this matter, we have co-operated with them just as we have done with Queen's University at Kingston where we have made a very excellent arrangement. As technical education is undoubtedly of great importance to the country, I have no doubt that when conditions become normal, the matter will have to be dealt with in a large way.

Has the minister asked the directors of the technical college at Halifax to develop some public interest in this phase of education? I know it is a very difficult problem, and I am sorry to say it is too true that there appears to be a much lesser interest on the part of young men to secure certificates of competency than there was twenty-five or thirty years ago. The mariners who occupy the high positions do not seem to be as well qualified as were the men of many years past, and that is rather strange, because there is a large demand for men and splendid positions are open for those who will qualify. I do not pretend to be able to give to the minister the solution of the problem. I know in my own province there should be. hundreds of men willing to qualify for marine service, but the truth is that very few have any desire to do so. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has been for a long time developing the theory of establishing a number of small schools, thinking numbers might be induced in that way to qualify. I have always expressed a doubt; I think in a province like Nova Scotia, if there was one big school, then notwithstanding the expense you would probably have a very large attendance, and the association of seafaring men with one another in numbers is an incentive to proficiency and efficiency. I admit, however, there is a great deal in the position taken by the hon. member for Guysborough. This is an important matter and the minister need not be alarmed at interfering because education is a provincial matter. After all, this is more a Dominion matter than a provincial one. It relates to trade and commerce. I do not think a marine education would come under the heading of education in the British North America Act. If the minister would entrust the Director of the Technical College at Halifax with the responsibility of starting and carrying on a propaganda in the Maritime Provinces for the purpose of encouraging young men to qualify for the marine service, I think he would be more likely to achieve success than by any other means. I think the Technical College at Halifax is the most efficient in the Dominion. I know that Mr. Sexton, the director, is a highly skilled and efficient man, and very greatly interested in his work. I am sure he would carry out the work zealously and intelligently, and I think he might achieve some success.

I do not want the minister to think we are talking merely for a pastime, because we are really very much in earnest. I think this work could be done without much expense. The same work is being done successfully and with very little expense in connection with the coal mining industry. There are local schools in all the mining towns in Nova Scotia where young men can attend in the evening and qualify for positions of foremen, etc. By arrangement with the local authorities, the high schools are used for the purpose. No rental is paid, and I believe that a great many of the men who are teaching the scientific branches of the steel and coal industry are giving their services free. This form of education would be of immense advantage to the people in the larger towns in the province of Nova Scotia, and I hope the minister will get the Director of the Technical College at Halifax to work out a scheme in co-operation1 with the high schools of the province. That would be a first step. If the scheme were not satisfactory the minister could turn it down, but I think Mr. Sexton will be able to devise some scheme which could be worked at least along the coast of Nova Scotia. Will the minister do this?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will give every consideration to what my hon. friend says.
Removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $20,000.
How much is being spend on this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our expenditure for the year ending March 31 last was $1,870. We have to have this item in the Estimates, because a large steamer might get wrecked at any time in an important channel, and the owners might be unable to remove it; in that case the department would remove it, and make the owners pay afterwards.
Inspection of live stock shipments, $5,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Our department is responsible for seeing that proper accommodation is provided on board ship for live animals. At one time we had inspectors at different ports throughout the country, but there has been such a small shipment of livestock of late years that these inspectors have been withdrawn, and the vote is accordingly very much decreased. Our expenditure last year was $2,401, and this was mostly spent at

Montreal in connection with the shipment of horses.
Was that amount paid to inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Part of it. Mr. Delorme, inspector at Montreal, receives an annual salary of $1,200; $300 was spent for office' rent, and there were miscellaneous expenses. Mr. Delorme sees that proper accommodation is provided.
What about the port of St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is practically no livestock shipped from St. John.
Lots of horses have been shipped from there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They were for war purposes and were looked after by Captain Lindsay, a paid official loaned to the Militia Department by the Marine Department. Captain Lindsay is superintendent of pilots on the St. Lawrence river.
He does not come in your estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Has the cattle trade died out altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This matter was taken up when we were in England with Mr. Pro-thero, the head of the Agricultural Department. Only a few days ago he stated in the House of Commons that there is no justification for excluding Canadian live cattle on the ground of disease.

That refers to stockers.
A great many cattle are shipped over there to be slaughtered on arrival.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes. Formerly, cattle used to be sent over and fattened in England. That was stopped by the Department of Agriculture, on the ground that there was disease among Canadian cattle. It has been proved time and again that there was no disease among Canadian cattle, that there was less disease among Canadian herds than among British herds. Mr. Prothero told us that there was no justification whatever for excluding Canadian cattle on the ground of disease.
The statement he made in the House of Commons a few days ago was published in the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. There is no doubt that the exclusion of Canadian cattle was 
largely a measure of protection for the stock raisers and breeders of Great Britain.
Mr. Prothero practically *admits that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Whether they will exclude our cattle as a measure of protection for their own stock raisers I do not know, but the stigma on our herds has been entirely removed, and I presume it will be followed by the removal of the embargo.

I take it for granted
that not many cattle are shipped, as the law calls for them to be slaughtered on landing.
Mr. HA-ZEN: Very few in the last year, I think.

I think this is
a very proper expenditure for the Department of Agriculture, but it is so small as to make one fear'that the inspection is a very careless one.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.
There should be a very rigid inspection in a matter of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspector goes very
carefully through the boat, inspects the conditions provided for the animals, what arrangements are made for a proper supply of water, and so on.
Is there any control over him, or' is it the case of a man who simply draws a salary, with nobody in the Government service to know or care whether he performs his duties or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He always reports to the department.

What does the
department do to satisfy itself that his inspection is a proper one?
Mr. HAZElN:	I think the inspeotdom at
Montreal must be very strict, for we have had complaints from the steamship company that this man is too exacting.
I am glad to hear that.

At the port of North
Sydney a good many cattle are shipped that come by the Intercolonial. I suppose the inspector at Montreal would have nothing to do with these shipments. What care is taken by the Government that these animals shall be properly looked after pending their shipment on the steamer? Sometimes

these cattle come in the (latter part of M.arc'h or April when the weather is stilil vea-y eold. They are taken from the cars, hut may have to wait a day or two before being put on shipboard. I know that people interested in the protection of dumb animals are much concerned to see that these cattle are not neglected. I presume that the accommodation on the boat is all right, but means to care for the cattle before they are put aboard the boat should be provided.
(Mr. HAZEN:	My attention has never
been called to this matter before. This certainly would not be the duty of the inspector at Montreal, for his duty and that of the other inspectors is to see to it that there is proper accommodation for the cattle aboard the ships. I do not know who would be responsible in the case to which, the hon. gentleman refers, but I will make inquiry.
The Railway Act provides for that, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I believe it does.
Mr. MeKENZIE: The inspector who was at North Sydney has gone to the war, and I am not aware that any officer has been appointed to replace him. Up to the time of his leaving, and for many years, inspection was carried on at North Sydney.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspector referred to was not an officer of my department. If a veterinary, he may have been an officer of the Department of Agriculture.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
Customs-Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion, including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding " anything in the Civil Service Act, and temporary Customs buildings and rentals, $3,590,000.

I wish the minister
would explain about this overwork and driving through the Civil Service Act. Of course, we know that the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) thinks little of the Civil Service Act; but, as he has practically unrestricted sway on the outside where he has thousands in the employ of the Customs who are not under the Civil Service Act, could he not give an approximate compliance with the Act as regards the remnant in the inside service? Ordinary departments, such as that of the Minister of Railways and Canals, have practically nobody in the outside service, except the employees of the Intercolonial railway which is managed as a railway and not strictly as part of the Civil Service. As all hon. members know who want to place those who cannot pass the Civil Service examination, and to find niches for friends, the minister has had a chance to appoint thousands to the outside service without reference to the Civil Service Act, which he has a right to do, but having this advantage over his colleagues who are not able to do it, has he any excuse for violating the Act with reference to the inside service? What does this mean?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext: This is not the inside service.
It says, " notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act."
As I understand the application of the Civil Service Act to employees of the Customs Department in the outside service
It is not like the inside service.

It is in this way: the Civil Service Act was passed by Parliament many years ago for the outside service, and it placed the outside customs officers under that Act. The employees in Broekville or ' Prescott are what we call outside employees. Under the Civil Service Act; if the law had been lived up to, you could not have appointed a man to a position in either of these towns unless he had passed the Civil Service examination.
He might be a temporary landing waiter or something of that kind.

I was going on to explain how it was done. Employees in the office are supposed to be called clerks and they have to pass an examination. The employees at the wharves or stations are called landing waiters, and they had to pass the Civil Service examination to be employed as landing waiters. That was carried on for a number of years. By the Customs Act the positions of collector of customs and preventive officer are excepted. Preventive officers were exempt, for the reason that they were employees supposed to do other work than that of clerks or landing waiters. Our secret service is under the preventive service. You might have to employ some special man and so on. Then the- Civil Service Act limited you so that you could

not employ a person over 35 years of age. You can appoint a preventive officer at any salary and any age; he is exempt. It is the same as it is under the Inland Revenue Act; certain officers there are excepted, although they are all under the Civil Service Act. I do not know whether the law was violated previous to 1896.
Previous to 1896-yes.

However, it does not make any difference as far as that is concerned. When there is a vacancy in the outside service- in many cases, not always-the recommendation is simply that so-and-so be appointed, and he has been appointed as a preventive officer and in many instances we have required an examination. Since I have been administering the Customs Department, the line I have taken is this-
A kind of crooked line- not straight.

It is a straighter line than had been followed for some time previously. I have been living as near as possible to the Civil Service Act with reference to examination in the outside service. Previous to the war I tried in almost all cases to get young men. Then, I always had an examination made by the collector or by our inspector to see if, in the opinion of the inspector or the collector, the applicant was qualified. The doctor's certificate, of course, was necessary under the Civil Service Act. That has helped us to get men who were really qualified for the positions.
What about the patronage committee?

In my county I am the patronage committee. That has been the policy I have followed and if any man passes the Civil Service examination he is promoted and given the position of clerk where the salary is higher than for a preventive officer. I think that answers my hon. friend's question.

While the minister seems to be in good huimour, I would like to ask him if the time has not arrived to remedy an injustice done after the general election of 1911 on the recommendation of Mr. Tan-crede Marsil of Montreal, who was my opponent in that election?
Did the Minister of Customs accept his recommendation?
Yes.

It is worse than I
thought.

He dismissed a man
named H. Hamel from the position of assistant appraiser. Mr. Hamel had a salary of $1,300. He had been named a preventive officer at a salary of $1,000 a year, and a year or two afterwards he was given an increase of $200, and he remained in the same position as assistant appraiser, doing the same work as he had done before 1911, and he is doling to-day the same work as he had done for years and years. He is a good officer, he has passed the Civil Service and promotion examinations and I am sure that the Minister of Customs will be just enough to remedy the injustice that he did on the recommendation of Mr. Tancrede Marsil after the general election of 1911, now that Mr. Tancrede Marsil has returned to the old Liberal party with which he pretended to be associated, and now that he has finished with the Nationalists. I hope the minister will remember the recommendation I made to him a few years ago, will recognize that the service of Mr. Hamel is of value to the department, and will give him the position he had before.

While at the moment I do
not remember the circumstances of this case, I shall look up the case and if there has been any injustice it will certainly be remedied.

The reason for the minister's action was that after the general election in 1911 Mr. Tancrede Marsil convinced the minister that Mr. Hamel had canvassed, some electors in Montreal to vote for me in Bagot. I had no electors in Montreal in 1911, and I can prove that statement at any time; the allegation was an absolute untruth. But Mr. Hamel was my brother-in-law and Mr. Tancrede Marsil recommended his dismissal as assistant appraiser apparently for that Teason. But as they needed Mr. Hamel in the department in Montreal, they made him preventive officer, and he is still in that position with the same salary.
Was he dismissed.?
As assistant appraiser.

He was dismissed as
assistant appraiser and nominated as preventive officer, but he was reduced from $1,300 to $1,000.

There is a Hector Hamel
drawing $1,200.
Yes, he was given an increase of $200 about two years ago, after I had represented to the minister the injustice that had been done him.

I now remember my hon.
friend speaking to me, but I thought that we had at least partially remedied the grievance of which he complained. The change from the position of assistant appraiser to that of preventive officer does not necessarily mean that the official has been degraded. However, if my hon. friend ie not satisfied, I shall look into the matter again, and if any injustice has been done to Mr. Hamel I shall be glad to remedy it.
That is all I recommend.

Will the minister say
he will not be prejudiced by any recommendation Mr. Tancrede Marsil may make?
I do not remember him making any.

He was the defeated
Conservative candidate, and so he would have the patronage in Montreal.

As he has returned to the Liberal fold, as my hon. friend has said, of course we have no choice in the matter.
Mr, MARCILE: The so-called Liberal.
My hon. 'friend is trying to return him, but he is not deceived.

The preventive officer at Boyleston, in Nova Scotia, Mr. Arthur Steele, was dismissed, I think, last year. It was very convenient for people in that district to be able to register their ships without having to travel five or six miles to Guysborough to enter their vessels. Is it the intention to appoint another officer at that port?

Since the commencement of the war I have been reducing the staff as much as possible, and where vacancies have occurred I have not filled them unless it was absolutely necessary. The money thus saved I have used to increase the salaries of customs officials in ports where the work of the department has been increased owing to the war. The cost of living has become so high that the salaries paid seem very small. Then it must be remembered that in many ports where there was some shipping before the war there is now little or none, owing to the scarcity of tonnage.
I am not urging an appointment; I am simply asking for information as to the minister's intention.
, I am not making appointments where I can avoid it.

I am glad to know that the minister is taking an economical view of these appointments, because, so far as I can learn, he has been very extravagant in this respect, possibly the greatest sinner among the ministers. From the public accounts he will find that in 1910-11 the expenditure of the Customs Department amounted to $2,187,174. During the last fiscal year, ended March 31, the expenditure in the same department was $3,685,399, an increase from 1910-11 of $1,498,225, or, roughly speaking, a million and a half of dollars. I do not think there is any justification for this enormous increase, which arises very largely, as I believe, from a reckless increase in the number of the staff. My hon. friend attempted to justify this last year and the year before, but I do not think that he succeeded. While there is no special increase this year, I should like the minister to explain the enormous increase, amounting to $1,500,000, in the cost of the administration of his department since he took office.

In the year 1910 the customs revenue was $87,596,426, and the cost of collection was 2.79 per cent. In the last fiscal year the revenue was $147,000,000, and the cost of collection was 2.64 per cent. Last year we had to increase our staff very materially on account of war conditions. In addition to 'that, over 200 men who enlisted prior to November, 1915, are being paid their salaries by the Customs Department.

In the case of those
whose salaries as Customs officials exceed their military pay, do you charge only the difference against the department, or is it the custom to show the whole pay in the departmental returns?

We charge the difference
against the department. Of course, in the case of those enlisted before November, 1915, the whole pay is charged <to the Customs Department. Many of our men who have gone to the front were receiving quite large salaries in the Customs Department-probably more than they receive in the militia. One splendid man, our chief accountant, Major Rorke, who has been in the department a great many years, enlisted at the commencement of



the war and is receiving his full pay as a customs official as well as his military pay.

I do not agree with the principle laid down by the minister that because of an increase in the revenue there should be a corresponding increase in the official staff. Unless new offices were established in various parts of the country, the fact that a larger business had been done would not justify my hon. friend in increasing the staff to such a large extent. The Minister of Finance handled a billion dollars of gold last year, but, as far as I know, he did not increase his staff. But I do not think the Minister of Customs has opened many new offices; I rather think that he is overcrowding the offices in the cities and small towns. Soon after he took charge of the department he dismissed a young man in my town for the reason that there was not enough for him to do, and shortly afterwards he appointed two stalwart men, friends of his own party, to fill the place formerly occupied by the man who had had nothing to do. Many instances of the kind could be cited in respect of other parts of Canada as well, I attribute a large part of the increase to things of that kind.

At some of the large ports, 'especially on the coast, we had to increase the staff after the commencement of war. Moreover, our staff was increased through the employment of secret service men in connection with the war. I have already said that 232 men who enlisted prior to November, 1915, are receiving their full salaries. These men have had to be replaced, because they have come from offices from which they could not very well be spared. The hon. member refers to a case in North Sydney.
I was referring to New Glasgow.

I do not remember that case, but I do know that I have not put on a man at any port unless I was very strongly urged to do so by the chief inspector, the inspector, or the collector. In every case I have tried to keep the number of men employed at the different ports down as low as possible, having due regard to the interests of the service. I do not think that the hon. gentleman can point to one case where I have put on a man whose services were not absolutely necessary, and any hon. gentleman who has had anything

to do with the Customs Department will bear me out in that. I do not admit that at any port in the Dominion we have put on more men than are required.

I do not wish to take up the minister's time unnecessarily, but I would like to understand a little more clearly the position of men who have joined the army and that of men who have not done so. As I understand it, up to a certain time-and the minister did not mention the time-all men who enlisted were paid not only their salaries from the Customs Department, but their salaries from the Militia Department. The money that was paid by the Militia Department does not appear as salary in the Estimates of my hon. friend, but the money that was paid by his department to the men who have enlisted does so appear. My hon. friend paid the full salaries down to a certain period, and I would like to know what that period was. After that period, he paid the difference between the militia salary and the salary received from the Customs Department, if there was a difference in the favour of the man who enlisted, and he charged to his own department that difference, but the money paid by the Militia Department is charged up in the War Appropriations. Do I understand my hon. friend correctly?

Yes, I think my hon. friend is right. I will explain the matter again and perhaps make it a little clearer. Shortly after war was declared, an Order in Council was passed by which we agreed to pay the full salary of any official, not necessarily of the Customs Department but of any department of the Government, who went overseas, in addition to his military pay. Suppose an official at Woodstock or any other port enlisted for overseas service, his name is kept on the paylist and the Customs Department continues to pay his salary just as though he were here.
Up to what date?

We are continuing to pay it. I am discussing the position of the man who enlisted between August 4, 1914, when war was declared, and November 30, 1915, a period of over a year and three months. That man's pay goes on just as though he were working in the Customs Department. Of course, such men gave instructions that their cheques were to be handed over to some relative, and that was done. Two hundred and thirty-two men have enlisted in that way.

Have you appointed
others in their places?

In many oases we have done so. Many men enlisted from large cities, such as Montreal, Toronto, or Hamilton, where we had to have others to fill their places, but in other places we did not require to replace men who enlisted. Some time in November, 1915, an OrdeT in Council was passed that men who enlisted after November 30, 1915, would be sure of their departmental salary. For instance, if an official employed in the Customs Department were receiving a certain salary and he enlisted in the militia as a private or a lieutenant, and the amount the Militia Department paid him for his services in the militia did not amount to the salary he was receiving in the Customs Department, then we would supplement the militia salary by an (amount that would make his total salary the same as though he had remained in the customs service, and that difference that we pay we charge up to the port in which that man was employed when Ihe went overseas.
That would appear in your Estimates?
It appears in our Estimates as an expenditure under the Oustoms Department.
Will the minister give us the gross amount of that expenditure?
I have not that this evening, and I cannot say what that amount is.

If the argument is to be used as an explanation of the large increase in the expenses of the department we would like to know how much that (amounts to, and what expenditure has been incurred under that head. Perhaps the minister will bring us that when his estimates are up again.
I shall he very glad to bring that information for the hon. member.
When those men who have enlisted come 'back and return to work, do their salaries from both the Militia Department and the Customs Department still continue?

No. What happens is this: 'If an official of the Customs Department returns to Canada he will probably be invalided home. We have had some cases where men who have been wounded at the front have returned, and when they come back here they may go to the hospital and 117i
it may take them two or three months or more to regain their health to such an extent that they can resume their work. The Militia Department then give them their discharge, and they take up their positions again in the department and are paid only the one salary, the customs salary. Some of the men who return have been wounded and they may receive pensions.
What is the position if they are not wounded, but simply come home on furlough?

I have not come across any cases of that nature. I know one case of a young man who was wounded who came home, and probably there are more .cases like that. This young man was wounded in the leg and he received three months' furlough. He is at present at his home at London, but his salary is being paid just the same. He is returning to the front; in fact, I think he sails on Thursday. In a case of that kind, of course, we would pay the salary.

I wish to discuss with the minister the removal of Mr. F. D. Shaw from the position of Collector of Customs at Lethbridge on the ground of insubordination. I have not been able to get the papers produced in connection with the case, but I have some of thp correspondence here, and it strikes me that the reasons for removing Mr. Shaw are not based on a very good foundation. Mr. Shaw had been in the customs service for over twenty years, and in August last he was removed from his position at Lethbridge on the ground of insubordination; that, without the sanction of the department at Ottawa he had placed a man in a position in the Lethbridge office. It is true that Mr. Shaw did place a man in a position in the Lethbridge office without the sanction of the department, but he did so on the recommendation of Mr. W. S. Ball, the gentleman who is in charge of the patronage in the constituency of Medicine Hat. This is the letter that Mr. Shaw addressed to the Commissioner of Customs in regard to the matter:
Lethbridge, Alta., 28 Aug., 1916. Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-
The following was handed me on the 26th inst. by Mr. Victor McGuire:
"I wish to -recommend Victor McGuire to fill the place recently vacated by F. G. Wad-dington.
(Sgd.) W. S. Ball."

Mr. McGuire reported kere on the 26th inst., and I asked him to call Mdnday, which he did, and I have taken him on the staff of this office temporarily, subject to your approval. My action in doing so was that he might be posted in some of the port work as Officer Burnett will be applying for his leave shortly.
I called on Mr. Ball this a.m., but found him out of town and could get no further information, but his partner said Mr. Ball had probably received word to appoint Mr. McGuire.
Mr. Shaw appointed this man solely on the recommendation of the gentlemen in charge of the patronage, and he has been removed from office on the ground that he had no right to make this appointment. As soon as Mr. Shaw had been removed, Mr. Ball, the Conservative candidate, who had charge of the patronage, wired the department assuming full responsibility for the appointment of McGuire. This is his telegram to the Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa:
Sir,-*
On August 26th, in reply to your letter asking me to recommend a man in Waddington's place, I wrote you recommending V. McGuire, and also wrote Mr. Shaw to same effect. I take full responsibility for this action and wish Mr. Shaw reinstated at once. There are no returned soldiers to fill Waddington's position.
(Sgnd.) W. S. Ball.
I understand that one of the reasons given by the department for removing Mt. Shaw was that they felt that any vacancies should be filled by returned soldiers. But there were no returned soldiers there at that time, and Mr. Shaw, acting on the advice of the gentleman in charge of the patronage, placed Mr. McGuire in the position. He advised the department that he had done so, and later on was notified that he had been removed on account of insubordination. As I have said, Mr. Ball immediately notified the department that he was wholly responsible, having asked Mr. Shaw to appoint McGuire temporarily, pending ratification from Ottawa. Those are the circumstances, and still Mr. Shaw is out of his position, and, so far as I know, there is no possibility of his being reinstated. It may have been a rule of the department that no person should be taken on the staff without sanction from the department at Ottawa. I understand, however, that there have been cases previously where the patronage committee had recommended certain appointments, and the men had been taken on, and the department at Ottawa subsequently ratified the appointments. Mr. Shaw was in this position: he had to please either the local patronage committee or the depart-

ment at Ottawa, and from the experience all other officials in Lethbridge had had with the patronage committee, I am quite certain Mr. Shaw was anxious to please the patronage committee. Mr. Shaw was appointed, I believe, by the Government of the late Sir John A. Macdonald, and he had been in the Customs Department of Alberta from that time until last fall. In view of his long experience, and of the circumstances I have presented, I think it is only fair that he should at least be granted an investigation into the charges made against him, and I am sure that any impartial investigator with the facts before him that I have here, would not recommend his removal from office. Mr. Shaw had the reputation of being one of the best customs officers in the southern part of Alberta. He had been in the service for years, and had given satisfaction to the business community. But the department, without any regard to these circumstances, removed him from his position, and have not given him an opportunity of presenting his case before any impartial investigator. I am sure Mr. Shaw would be quite satisfied with an investigation into this particular case. From the evidence I have here, and from the conversations I have had with Mr. Shaw,' I am sure that he could establish that he was not at fault, and was simply acting on the request of the gentleman in charge of the patronage in the city of Lethbridge.
I understand that it has been charged that Mr. Shaw took similar action in a number of other instances, but he assures me that no complaint had ever been made against any appointments he had made on recommendations of this kind, and that in no time during his service in the Customs Department had any complaint been made against him as 'a customs officer. Mr. Ball assumes full responsibility for having recommended McGuire, and naturally Mr. Shaw wanted to satisfy the gentleman in charge of the patronage. He followed the usual course of advising the department that he was taking this man on, and following that he was removed from office.

Before I answer the hon.
member, I might- say to my hon. friend from Guysborough that the collections for New Glasgow in the fiscal year ending 1912 were $135,558, and the number of officers in that year was four. During the last fiscal year the collections amounted .to $800,878, and the number of officers was six. On account of the Bussian orders and so forth we had to put on extra men.

What were the figures
at the time these additions to the staff were made?

I can get that for my hon.
friend. As regards Mr. Shaw, he was appointed by the Conservative party, so there can be no question of a dismissal for political reasons.

Unless a younger and
more up to date fellow wanted his job.

The vacancy occurred some months ago, and I decided to follow our usual policy of appointing a returned soldier to the position. I am still holding the position open in the hope of getting a returned soldier to fill it; I think no one will object to that. The hon. member states that Mr. Shaw has been a satisfactory official, but I may say that Mr. Shaw did not give satisfaction to this department. I have had many complaints against him during the time I have been administering the department.
Mr. BU'OHANAN:	Has any complaint
been made that he did not give satisfaction as an officer?

Yes, parties have given me
that information.
That was npt the reason given for his removal.

This was not the first time
that Mr. Shaw had appointed any one he liked. If I remember rightly, my predecessor, through the Commissioner of Customs, reprimanded Mr. Shaw for appointing an official just as he did in this case, I think that a month or two before we did suspend him. He did not then carry out the instructions of the chief inspector. I understand from my officials that Mr. Shaw seemed to wish to run the port of Lethbridge irrespective of the department. Of course, you cannot run a department that way. So, Mr. Shaw was suspended. If I [DOT]remember rightly, he wrote to the department, or to myself, a very insulting letter, at a time when I was considering the taking up of his case again.

Was not that letter
written by a lawyer in Lethbridge?

It may be that a lawyer
wrote it for him, but I remember receiving a very insulting letter. Mr. Shaw certainly was deserving of suspension for the position he took after he was suspended. His dismissal was not for the purpose of putting
some friend of the party into his position, but because the officials of the Government thought he deserved dismissal. I have not accepted the recommendation of any one for appointment to that office, but am keeping it open, as I .am keeping other offices open, including some in my own county, for returned soldiers.

Did the minister take into consideration the wire that came from the gentleman handling the patronage, to the effect that he took full responsibility for the appointment of this gentleman to the staff?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Buchanan) knows that only the commissioner or the minister would have authority to say whether an official was required or not. I have always refused to take on an officer on the recommendation of any one without first having him examined to make sure that he is qualified for the position.

Had not the other
course been permitted .in the office of the port of Lethbridge?

Not so fax as I am aware.
The position I have taken ever since I began administering the department is that there must be an examination by the inspector or, if deemed better under special circumstances, by some other high official, such as the Collector, before an appointment is made. If a man is appointed without an examination, he may prove to be not qualified for the office, and then there is difficulty in dispensing with his .services. So far as my memory .goes, we have never appointed an officer at Lethbridge without an examination. There may have been exceptions, hut I do not recollect any.

I am pretty intimately acquainted with the business community in Lethbridge, and I never heard any complaints against Mr. Shaw as an officer, but since his removal I have heard 9 p.m. many expressions of dissatisfaction with the Government's action in his case. The minister speaks of an insulting letter he received, written on behalf of Mr. Shaw. I think I can explain that without mentioning the name of the writer. There is in Lethbridge a very warm admirer of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), an old acquaintance of his from .Nova Scotia, and when Mr. Shaw was removed this gentleman was so indignant that he wrote not only to the

Prime Minister tout also to the department. He did not write as a lawyer representing Mr. Shaw, tout as an indignant Conserwar tive of Lethbridge, and he is so indignant that I doubt very much whether this Government will receive his support in the next general election. That is where the "insulting letter" came fjroim. And the writer of that letter is not alone; there is great dissatisfaction amongst many leading supporters of the Government over the removal of Mr. Shaw. If there was any complaint in the business community of Lethbridge against the conduct of Mr. Shaw in office, I never heard of it. I have heard of a very powerful concern operating in Southern Alberta objecting to his actions, and they probably have made complaint, but I understand that those complaints are not to his discredit, for he was simply carrying out the regulations of the department. As to his removal, Mr. Shaw's position is simply this:	They have in Lethbridge a patronage committee, and unquestionably he was afraid of that committee and was trying to do all he could to satisfy it. When he took this gentleman on the staff, on the recommendation of the patronage committee, I think he felt warranted in doing so; in fact he felt that should he fail to carry out their instructions they would use their influence at Ottawa to have him removed. And now the department dismisses him for that action. I venture to say that in any ordinary business concern a man who had acted as Mr. Shaw had acted, under the conditions that faced him, would be reinstated. I do not, think the removal was fair. Mr. Shaw was entitled to an investigation, and, had his case been investigated by an impartial investigator, I am confident recommendation would have been made for his reinstatement.

The minister has told us that he is keeping a number of offices for returned soldiers. In the town of Brock-ville he has made an appointment of one returned soldier, which appointment meets the approval of every person.
I have appointed three.
There is one that I remember. Can the minister tell us how many returned soldiers he has appointed, what is their status, and what is the aggregate of their salaries?

I could not give the aggregate, of their salaries, but up to the end of April 203 appointments of returned soldiers had been made, at salaries averaging $900 to
	'
$1,000 a year. And others are being appointed.

There is one office, I have been told, which is being kept for a returned soldier-the collectorship of the port of Montreal. It seems to be a question whether the port of Montreal collectorship or the port of Toronto collectorship is vacant, for, on the resignation of Mr. White in Montreal, Mr. Bertram, of Toronto, was sent to Montreal. In my personal communication with people of Montreal, while they have no fault' to find with Mr. Bertram as an official, yet they cannot understand why it is necessary to take an official from Toronto to succeed an official in Montreal. They have been told that Mr. Bertram is to return to Toronto, but there is nothing definite as to time or occasion. The situation is a very peculiar one, and if there is a precedent for it I cannot lay my hand on that precedent at the present time. When certain Conservatives of Montreal have approached the department as to whether there was any person in the province of Quebec competent to succeed Mr. White they have been told that the collectorship of Montreal was being reserved for a returned soldier. Could the minister give us any idea as to what soldier he has in mind?

Montreal is the most important port in Canada and it is very important at the present time on account of war conditions. When it became vacant I suggested, that, like other vacancies, it should go to a returned soldier. It was my first intention to send Mr. H. C. Blair, who is one of our best inspectors, to Montreal.
Where is he?

He is from Ottawa. I sent him to Toronto for this reason: the man had just lost his son at the front and Toronto is not as hard a port to manage at the present time as is Montreal. I asked if Mr. Bertram could go to Montreal and take charge until a returned soldier would' come back because it required a first class man. If the hon. gentleman knows Mr. Bertram, he will agree with me that there is no man in Canada better qualified to fill the position than Mr. Bertram. I explained to Mr. Bertram that I wanted him to take that place until a soldier came back. There is no man-no returned soldier-in my mind that I intend to appoint to that position. I am waiting until they come back.

But there are a number of prominent Montreal men who are qualified to fill that position and who are now over at the front. I have heard the names of one or two wounded officers who have been at the front, who have taken a great part and who have received honours for bravery. I have said that if one of these men-I do not care which-returns and is qualified to fill that position, he will be appointed and Mr. Bertram will then return to the city of Toronto. The hon. member knows that if you are holding a vacancy of that kind for a returned soldier, it is better to get some one from outside to fill the place temporarily than to ask one of the officials of the port to take it. If you promote him to the position of collector, it is hard to change him back to the position that he might have occupied before. In addition to that, the number of men on the staff in Montreal who may be qualified to fill that position is limited. While I am administering the Customs Department I will fill any vacancies in that department by the appointment of those who have been injured in France. No matter whether it is the position of collector of Customs of Montreal, which is the highest salaried position in the Custom service. I will hold it for a returned soldier.
I am glad to hear the minister make that public announcement; really that is what I was after.
I made it before.
Not so publicly. I wanted to get it on record because these things are better when they are really official and the public understand them.
I made this very same statement in the House and it is on Hansard.

Perhaps I was not here, but the people of Montreal are still incredulous. There are certain Conservatives in Montreal who believe that the minister is keeping this position open for a wounded soldier, but it is to be a wounded political soldier who may now be in the Government and who is going to be wounded in the house of his friends politically. Some people think that this position is being retained with the idea that somebody, some minister-not necessarily my hon. friend- may find it possible to discover himself after readjustment time comes in the weeks that are to follow. I wanted to get the hon. gentleman to publicly admit that it is a soldier who, as he says, has been in France
and has returned. I was delighted to hear the minister say that it was to be reserved for a soldier wounded on the European battlefield and that it was not being kept for a soldier wounded in the Government at Ottawa or something of that kind. Now that it has been so clearly defined, the people of Montreal can rest assured that Mr. Bertram is to stay there only until some returned soldier who is qualified, and is a resident of Quebec, will get the appointment.
If he returns while I am administering the department, he will.

He may have to come back very soon. My hon. friend's successor in office may be a person who is not in sympathy with the view of my hon. friend. I want to make sure that it is a returned soldier who is going to get this position in Montreal because that is what my hon. friend has said. What he has announced to-night will help somewhat to steady the feeling in Montreal which is not very sure-I am not positive that it will be sure yet-but in so far as the minister can say, his statement has limited the opportunity for appointment during the next few weeks because he gives us the assurance that it will be a returned soldier who will get the position. Can the minister give us the assurance that that is to be the Government's policy? I do not mean that it is only to be his policy because ministers may go and ministers may come but the Government may remain if it can do so by its own vote and I am anxious to know if that is to be the policy of the Government or if it is to be deviated from if the minister goes out. I want to commit the Conservative Government to this policy with regard to the port of Montreal and not the minister individually because he may not have the power.

As far as the people of Montreal are concerned, I do not think they are very much troubled as to who will fill this position. I have not any doubt at all that if my health keeps good I will fill the position of Minister of Customs for many years. I am not a bit alarmed about what will happen, 1
You mean you will attempt to fill it.
I am satisfied that I will sit on this si'de of the House and fill the position of Minister of Customs.
Not fill it-you do not mean that?

As far as the Collector of Customs is concerned, when I say that as a member of the Government it will be filled by a returned soldier, it means that the Government will carry out that policy and fill it by the appointment of a returned soldier. I only hope and trust that if the hon. member comes into power, if he get3 on this side, he will give the returned soldiers the same treatment that I am giving them as Minister of Customs.

I am glad to draw that, too, because it is very illuminating. My hon. friend a moment ago, very carefully assured us that "so long as I am Minister of Customs," refraining from committing the Government to it as a matter of policy, he would do a certain thing. Now he has committed the Government and I am satisfied that, in so far as the Government of which he is a member will have power when the time comes, they will appoint a returned soldier to the position.
Does that apply to the other departments of the Government as well as to the Customs Department?
So far as I know, it does.

I wish to refer to the conditions in my own town of North Sydney. I am not going to say much about the number of officials appointed by the minister. He has increased the staff, I think, about 200 per cent. But I have another fault to find with the minister, and that is that he has not treated fairly in the matter of promotions the officials whom he found in office as compared with the favourites of the Conservative party who werfe appointed to office after this Government came into power. I think that when an old official is doing his work well he has a right to be treated exactly in the same way as the new man who comes into office under a different Administration. The minister told us that nobody was appointed to any position except upon the recommendation of either the chief officer of customs at the port where the appointment was to be made, or of some customs official or inspector. I can tell the minister how these recommendations were made, so far as the chief officers were concerned. They were made simply because those men an many instances were Liberals, holding their offices after the change of Government by the grace of the Minister of Customs and some Tory ward

heelers who had the power of dismissal and appointment in their hands, as they believed they had and as I have no doubt they had. When they wanted anybody appointed they would simply go to the customs officer, take him by the throat and say: Here, I am told that if you recommend me to office I will be appointed. Then the customs officer had no alternative; he had no soul of his own; he was trying to protect his own head, and he would give that letter of recommendation that such and such a man should be appointed. That is the way those recommendations came to the minister, and he will find on inquiry that they were given simply because they were demanded by parties who wanted to be appointed to office. In North Sydney he will find that there were only five officials doing the whole work of the department in 1911 before the change of Government. To-day there are ten men doing the same work. I submit that there was no increase in the revenue at the port of North Sydney that would justify such a large increase in the number of officials appointed to do that work. My complaint is in reference to one of the oldest officers there, an officer named McDonald, a good official, a man against whom there has never been one black mark, so far as faithful service to the department is concerned. The moment the change of Government took place, there ceased to be any notice given to him or any advance in his pay. Younger men who came into the service nine or ten years after his appointment, are to-day enjoying larger salaries than he is enjoying, and they have been advanced in their pay year after year since their appointment. Since the change of Government, Mr. McDonald stands out as a marked man, and not one dollar of increase has been given to him. I submit that this is not fair treatment, I was going to say that it was not manly treatment, and if recommendations for increases of salary are made as the minister says,-by officers in his own department, I want to know by what philosophy or what sense of smell, if I may use the expression, they can detect from the Customs Department here at Ottawa the difference between John McDonald and the other officials in the town of North Sydney, so that they can promote all others who are Tories and leave McDonald behind. This I feel should be brought to the attention of the minister, and I do not think he can defend conduct of that kind. I would also want to know why, when the offices were not enlarged, with the same buildings, the

same work, the same offices, it was necessary to have ten men to do the work which was accomplished and satisfactorily performed by five men in 1911. At the town of Sydney Mines the same thing occurs. There was only one man there before and there has been an increase of 100 per cent; there are now two men doing the work of one, possibly on the recommendation of -somebody who wanted to get a position, when one would have been sufficient. I submit that too many appointments have been made and that unfair treatment has been meted out to the Liberals who had been occupying positions before the change of Government took place.

I hardly think the hon. member is fair in his criticism in so far as that port is concerned. He stated there were ten men on the pay-lists at that port instead of six. In counting the ten he is including Mr. Brennan, who is overseas, and of course is not at work at that port, so it would mean nine men, or an increase of three men. I find that on the 16th of May, 1912, the collector ot North Sydney w-rote the department that the Reid-New-foundland line intended placing an additional vessel on the route between Port aux Basques and North Sydney, making a daily service, and they wanted another man to attend to that service.
That is just what I say, a man wanted the office and he made the collector write the letter.

In addition to that, on the 29th January, 1915, the collector wrote the department asking for the appointment of " an officer whose duty would be to board all shipping and report same, and keep records and make annual reports to the 'depairtalent, subject to the collector as Officer Foran had to spend most of his time at inside work." Then, on account of war conditions, it was necessary to have extra employees at that port. So far as the treatment of officers is concerned, the hon. member states that I have not treated the Liberal officers fairly, or that I have given preference to those whc have been appointed since the change of Government. I have before me the record of the staff at North Sydney. The collector is Joseph McPherson, who receives a salary of $1,600 per annum, overtime $295, and for services in connection with Inland Revenue, $347. Mr. Brennan is overseas; we pay him his salary, $950. Mr. J. H. Cameron was appointed in 1913 as appraiser and gauger at
$1,200 a year. I would say that that is not a large salary for the position.
How did you get along previously without that official?

The Commissioner of Cusr
toms, who was there himself and looked into the matter recommended the employment of an appraiser and gauger at North Sydney. Mr. John Cogan was appointed in May, 1914, at a salary of $800; his overtime pay last year was $281.10. Mr. McDonald, who, with Mr. Cogan, is acting as landing waiter, receives a salary of $800; his overtime pay last year was $284.10. These gentlemen, one a Liberal appointee, and the other a Conservative, are receiving practically the same salary. Mr. David Edwards, clerk, receives $900 a year; his overtime last year was $292.80. Clerks rank higher in the service than landing waiters, and receive a higher salary. Mr. F. E. Jackson receives $1,000 and his last year's overtime was $308.10. He is a clerk in the long room. Mr. James McLeod, whose salary is $800, does not appear to have received any overtime pay. Mr. Hector W. McNeil was appointed in 1915; last year he received $900 as salary and $124.20 as overtime. His salary and overtime, therefore, amount to less than the remuneration given to Mr. McDonald or to Mr. Cogan. Mr. Angus Young, who patrols the harbour, boards vessels, and reports same, received $1,000 and $499.50 overtime. That is the whole of the North Sydney staff. The salaries paid to the landing waiters are the same as those paid prior to the war; they are the salaries of that class. I have taken up the matter of increasing the salaries of those who receive less than $900; if this matter had come up a few days later, the landing waiters at North Sydney would probably have been among those recommended for an increase. Having regard to war conditions, the salaries of many of the officials are really low. I feel very strongly that something should be done to help many of those who are getting these small salaries. In many instances we have been able to increase the salaries owing to the saving made in reducing the staff at certain places. Some proposed increases are now before Council, and from time to time we shall endeavour to increase the salaries of those who are in this $800 class.

The minister did not
explain the point of my criticism. He has not stated why every one of these ten men received an increase of salary except Mr. COMMONS
McDonald, who is the only Liberal among them. This action sh,ows that the partyism which has characterized my hon. friend's administration of the department ever since he took office has 'been visited upon this man McDonald. The man whom they got to perjure himself in an attempt to find fault against McDonald was committed to penitentiary fpr perjury. The minister did not explain who was appointed to meet the new boat. McDonald used to meet the boat when only one was running; if this man Mr. Edwards does anything outside he meets the other boat. McDonald has been in the service about 20 years, while Edwards has been in the service only a few years. Edwards gets a larger salary than McDonald simply because he is a pet of the Administration. McDonald is still in the service because those who were seeking to have him dismissed could find no other man to peTjure himself against him. The minister cannot defend his position; he might as well say: yes, we have singled this man out just as we single out everybody who is not a Conservative and try to starve him out of house and home.

I think that my hon. friend is hardly fair in his assertions. He says that I have increased the salaries of all those who have been appointed since we came into power. Mr. Cogan was appointed on May 18, 1914 at a salary of $800. This, w'ith the overtime, is practically the same as the amount received by Mr. McDonald.
Has length of service nothing to do with promotion?

I think it is hardly fair for
the hon. gentleman to say that we have promoted every man who was appointed by this Government and have allowed the Liberals to remain where they were. As to the additions to the staff, two of the new appointments were asked for, as I have said, by the collector of customs for the reasons stated. The collector wrote the commissioner urging that two men be appointed, but having regard to war conditions, we could not then see why they should be appointed at the present time. The commissioner, however, on his visit to North Sydney, after looking over the port, considered it was in the interest of the service that an appraiser should be appointed. All that I know about the matter is that the collector urged that two more men be appointed; the officials of the department acting on his advice, so far as I know, finally decided that those appoint-

ments were necessary, and we appointed the two men that I have named, and it was at the request of the commissioner that I appointed the appraiser. The hon. member is hardly fair in his criticism of me so far as filling the positions in that port or any treatment of the officers is concerned. As for Mr. McDonald, I cannot remember all the circumstances, but if Mr. McDonald was an appointee of the previous Government, he is still in his position, and if I had such a feeling as the hon. member states I have, I might have had him dismissed, but I retained him in that position.

As I stated, you could not get any evidence against him except that of a man who perjured himself and who was sent to the penitentiary for perjury. You did not dare to try the case against him the second time.
Do I understand that the Minister of Customs does not permit any politics to enter his mind in the administration of his department? Is that the rule?
Always the rule.

I wish the minister would consult me about customs matters in the port of Halifax, because I would be pleased to advise him, and I think I could give him very good advice. Might I have the promise that I shall be consulted about such matters in the future?
I have no objection to that, and I shall be very glad to have the hon. member's advice.
The minister will ask for your advice after an appointment is made.

I wish to make an inquiry for the purpose of eliciting some information in regard to a matter about which I know very little. In the British Columbia papers I have from time to time noticed that applications are made to the Department of Customs for the appointment of a customs official at the port of New York. I understand that the purpose of this requested appointment is to facilitate shipments originating on the Pacific coast to eastern Canadian points via American ports. To put the matter in a concrete form, I understand that if a shipper of Canadian produce on the Pacific coast desires to ship to the port of Montreal in the winter, he must tranship at some American port, and he desires that there be a Canadian customs official at that

port in order to facilitate transhipments and to enable him to escape some onerous customs regulations and, I suppose, the payment of duty. I do not pretend to be well informed on the matter, and I am rather anxious to understand exactly the nature of the request made by the Vancouver Board of Trade and the boards of trade of various towns of British Columbia. I wish the minister would be good enough to explain the details of the request and the position of the department on the matter.

For some little time there has been such an agitation in British Columbia. It was started, I believe, by the Maple Leaf line running from New York to San Francisco and Vancouver. What they asked the department to do was to place a customs officer at New York and allow them to ship their products, say from Ontario and the lower provinces, by rail to New York, where they would be placed in a vessel, for shipment to Vancouver. The Board of Trade, as I understand the matter, said that the shipments would be made only in British vessels. The bonding privileges between the two countries are carried on in this manner: the goods may be shipped from one point in Canada to another through American territory, but in such cases, the freight cars are sealed when they leave Canada, and when they re-enter Canadian territory, the seals are broken by a customs official, so that there is no question that the goods are in the same condition as when they left Canada. There were different reasons why I could hardly see that it would be in the interest of Canada to grant that request. One reason was that it would be difficult to carry it out in the way of bonding the goods, the same as we do in the case of goods shipped by rail, because when the goods left Canada they would be placed on a vessel, and the part of the vessel in which the goods were could not be sealed.
Might the goods not bear a mark?

You might.put a mark on
them, 'but still that mark might be obliterated. Another reason was this: we could not put an officer in the port of New York on the distinct understanding that the traffic between New York and Vancouver would be carried only by British vessels, because if we were to attempt to do that, we might create difficulties with the United States Government. Then again, it did not
seem to me to be fair that our products in eastern Canada, products that we feel British Columbia should have, and the products in British Columbia that we should have in eastern Canada, that is, goods that should be transported by water on account of the cheapness of the article, should have to be shipped from one part of the Dominion to the other, on foreign vessels, or by means of other transportation in the hands of foreigners. British Columbia and eastern Canada should have every facility of water transportation, but in the summer time shipments should be made in vessels coming to Montreal, St. John or Halifax. The port would be Montreal, if the goods came from Quebec or vicinity, and St. John or Halifax, if the goods came from the lower provinces. From those ports the vessels would carry the cargoes around to Vancouver, and vice versa when the freight is from the West the vessels would come from Vancouver to those ports that I have mentioned. After the war broke out it was impossible to get vessels to engage in that trade. Freight rates have gone up enormously, and I do not think there is any possibility of getting either British or American vessels for that service while the war is on.
That does not affect the principle at all.
It is, therefore, of no advantage to consider' the placing of an officer at New York at the present time.
I understand that British Columbia made a request for the appointment of such an official long before the war. The question is bound to come up again.

A request was made a short time before the war, but there were the objections that I have stated. Believing that it would be in the interests of our Atlantic and Pacific ports, I suggested to the Government that we give a contract for two vessels to start this service.
Will they be subsidized, or Government steamers?
Government steamers.

That will not meet the difficulty. In the case of a ship, for instance, landing at Halifax with a cargo destined for Toronto or Hamilton, the minister suggests that the cargo be landed at Halifax and proceed by rail to Toronto or Hamilton. Now the shipper might not be able to stand the railway rates. I am

speaking of the winter season, when the ships could not proceed to Montreal.

I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway rate from Hamilton to St. John is exactly the same as from Hamilton to New York. The railways give exactly the same rates to our Atlantic ports as to New York, and if a vessel arrived at Halifax with a cargo for Toronto or Hamilton the rate would he the same as from New York to those points.
But Halifax would not be so advantageous a port as New York for getting a return cargo.
The railway companies have agents all over the provinces looking for traffic.
Not for westbound traffic via the Panama Canal.
I mean return cargo for vessels.
The Canadian railways would not encourage that.

There is a lot of cheap freight that must be carried in that way. In the summer time there is a water route, for instance, from Montreal to Port Arthur, and a rail rate beyond, and the railways are looking for that traffic.

The Canadian railways surely would not encourage competition by giving a special freight rate from eastern Canadian points to New York. That would simply be encouraging traffic by water from New York to Vancouver. The minister's scheme would be of immense advantage in developing traffic if the steamers could get a return cargo from Halifax or St. John, but they are not likely to get it.

They are likely to get it from points in Ontario and other provinces. For instance, if a man had a cargo of timber at Vancouver which he wanted to ship to Hamilton, if we had an officer at New York he could get the American rate. The American railways have a rate right through to New York, and all the shipper would have to do would be to add the American rate to the water rate. The advantage to the railway companies is that they get the haul from Toronto or Hamilton to St. John or Halifax. The Canadian Pacific would get the traffic from Hamilton to St. John, the Government railway system from Ham-
[Mr. A. K. Maclean !
ilton to Halifax, the Canadian Northern or the Grand Trunk to Montreal, and the Intercolonial the balance. The railways must compete with that water traffic, and they do it in order to get a portion of the haul. This proposed service would encourage traffic between the Atlantic and Pacific ports through our own country, and it might also encourage traffic between the West Indies and Canada. I do not know the situation thoroughly, but it is possible that if a vessel had not a full cargo for Montreal she could take freight for the West Indies, and bring back sugar to this country. I do not think it will be possible to get vessels of any kind while the war is on. We have given a contract for two vessels, and I should like to see them built and in commission.
In what service?
From Vancouver to Halifax and St. John in the winter, and to Montreal in the summer.	,

My dear Mr. Minister, if you want to assist in building up traffic between eastern and western Canada, all you have to do' is to arrange with the United States authorities to put a Customs officer at New York, and they will do the rest, and they will do it a lot cheaper than you can, by any vessels you put on. I know what I am talking about, because I know the rates, and it is the New York rates that will bring the rate down and give us the accommodation.

I am not taking issue with that. Notwithstanding what the hon. member says I think I know what I am talking about too, and I believe I am absolutely right. I feel very strongly, much stronger than the hon. gentleman does, that it is in the interests of Canada, in the interests of Halifax and St. John, where we are enlarging the harbours, and in the interests of Vancouver, that every bit of freight we can carry between eastern and western points should be handled by our own men, by our own ships, and by our own railways. I believe also, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman says, that our Canadian vessels, our Canadian railways, manned by our Canadian citizens, can carry from Vancouver to Montreal as cheaply as Americans can.

I agree, but we are not
doing it. I am as loyal to our people and to our carriers as is the hon. gentleman, but when they want exorbitant rates, rates

so high that we cannot get our goods into the hands of the consumers at prices that they can afford to pay, then I say we want competition.

I was not taking issue with
the hon. gentleman on a question of loyalty, but I say that we can carry as cheaply as Americans can. He says we are not doing it, but I do not accept his statement; I believe we are doing it. I say that freight rates from Hamilton by our roads are the same as on American roads. We have never had a vessel route yet. It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to talk about rates being cheaper by way of New York, but he is speaking of the time before the war when vessels were running.
You can get them now.

No, I have made inquiries,
and I can tell the hon. gentleman that there are really no vessels there. To-day we are carrying freight on our railways at the same rates as via New York, and, as soon as we get these vessels we shall have the competition just as there has been in ordinary times, and I am confident that our Canadian vessels will carry at equally low Tates with the American vessels, and perhaps lower.

The minister says we
have two vessels under construction that may be used for this trade?
I said we gave a contract for two vessels.
To whom?
To two shipbuilding companies in Vancouver.
Ate they steel vessels?
No, wooden.
Freight vessels?
Yes.
The intention ie to use them on the route from Vancouver to Atlantic ports by way of the Panama canal? Are they steam or sailing vessels?
They have what is called auxiliary power. They run eight or nine knots an hour.
