That would be a very slow service. I cannot understand the hon. minister's explanation. His main reason seems to be that because one cannot send a whole shipload at one time it would not be advisable to send packet freight. But we
are now using the bonding privilege to send goods to the United States, and we do not need to send a whole carload, do we? One can send a locked trunk, can he not?
It goes in a bonded car.

I would not object to that. But if you can send such a package without violating the customs regulations, why not facilitate the traffic by having an officer in New York? Then it will be possible to put goods aboard a steamer running between Halifax and New York, or between Quebec and New York, and tranship them to another boat running through the Panama canal, and perhaps tranship again in order to reach Vancouver. Why should not these facilities be granted? The minister's reasons, so far as I can understand them, do not seem to be sound. And the remedy he proposes seems to me ridiculous. He is going to have auxiliary-power wooden sailing vessels put on the route. That would be the slowest kind of a
10 p.m. line that ever was and would never work up any trade worth while. I hope the minister is ambitious to do more than that.

I agree that it is desirable to confine to our own transportation lines, as far as possible, our domestic traffic. But here is a special condition which requires special treatment. I do not see anything strange in appointing customs officials at the port of New York to facilitate transhipment from vessels laden with cargo from Vancouver and destined for eastern Canadian points. One would need to understand better than I do the cargo that vessels sailing from eastern Canada to Vancouver would be likely to carry. It might not be possible to get a west-bound cargo at a Canadian port at all-I do not know that, but I say it is probable. But a Vancouver steamer can secure a return cargo at the port of New York, goods originating in Canada and reaching New York in bond. All the Vancouver people ask for is the same facilities for their products destined for eastern Canada.
No, they cannot ship to Canadian eastern ports through New York now.
But that steamer on her return trip can be loaded with Canadian goods which have come through American territory on American rails in bond?
No, they cannot do that.
Why not? Do I understand that Canadian goods cannot be shipped from a Canadian point to the port of New York, there to be loaded aboard a steamer bound to British Columbia without paying duty?
No; if they could do that, they could do the same thing back again.

I want to come back again to the appointment of returned soldiers. The minister will see in a moment why I was so anxious that he should commit himself and also commit his colleagues on this subject. I find in the London Advertiser the following despatch:
New Postmaster.
St. Marys Office Pilled, But Not by Returned Soldier.
St. Marys, May 27.-Bert L. Lancaster has been, appointed postmaster, vice T. O. Robson, who resigned through illness.
It was expected that Lincoln Rice, a Toronto University student and a returned soldier, would be given the appointment in view of the Government promise to give invalided soldiers, where qualified, such positions.
The Postmaster General, who -is in uniform, and has been on a recruiting tour in Quebec, is responsible for appointing a man, undoubtedly at the request of political friends, and declining to appoint a returned soldier as postmaster in St. Mary's. You can understand why, with that kind of a disposition, he would not make a successful recruiting officer, and the minister will be able to see the necessity and wisdom of my committing the Postmaster General to the policy of appointing returned soldiers, which policy has been violated by him no longer ago than on May 27.

The hon. member should
bring it up on Postmaster General's estimates. I do not know anything about it.

I certainly shall, but I wanted to point out to my hon. friend the l eason why I pursued him till Ihe committed the Government to the policy of appointing returned soldiers. His colleagues are not carrying out that policy.
There may be some explanation of that case.

In order to make sure, as my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has done in the case of Montreal, I might call the attention of the Minister of Customs to the fact that there is a vacancy at present at the most important port in the county of Gloucester, caused by the death

of Mr. John J. Harrington, late collector of customs at Bathurst, who died a few weeks ago. So far the position has not been filled. I would understand that it would be in order to appoint a returned soldier from the field of battle. I am willing to say that the Bathurst collector, although appointed by my hon. friend, was a very good officer, a good citizen, a good father and a man of high character, whose death caused regret to every citizen of Bathurst. - The officer who was dismissed in 1911 by my hon. friend is to-day a minister of the Crown in the new Liberal Government in the province of New Brunswick, and I suppose he owes a debt of gratitude to my hon. friend for his dismissal at that time. However, we shall see what the course of the minister will be when a returned soldier is available for that position. I admit that there is not among any of the returned soldiers to-day one who would be qualified for that position. Unfortunately, of those who have gone from my county, more have made the supreme sacrifice on the field of honour than have come back with laurels either wounded or incapacitated. Meanwhile I would like to make sure, as my hon. friend made sure in regard to Montreal, that I can depend upon it that my hon. friend will defer action until a returned soldier qualified to fill the position comes back. There is more than one man at the front to-day who is qualified for that position and any :ne of these men, when he come1 back, will be able to fid the position with honour and ability. There is one very young man who has returned with honours won upon the field of battle but he has not been offered the position. Of course, he happens to be the son of the dismissed officer who is now a minister of the Crown in the province of New Brunswick. My hon. friend is not aware, perhaps of all these details. Yet, in order to make sure as to what might take place in the future I want to secure the promise of my hon. friend that if he should be pressed by the politicians of Gloucester county, he will resist their demand until a returned soldier, able to fill the position, shall come back and that he will get the position.

I would have liked the hon. member (Mr. Turgeon) to have told the whole story about Bathurst as I recollect it. From the speech of the hon. member one might infer that in case there was a vacancy at Bathurst I would not appoint a returned soldier. I do not know whether

I am right or not, but is it a fact, or is it not, that there has been a vacancy at Bathurst and that I did insist upon a returned soldier who was not a resident of the county at all getting that position?
Yes, but I referred to the collectorship. That is the assistant.
Why did not the hon. member, in making these few remarks, explain the whole case because this goes to show that I am following up that policy right in the county in which he lives?

Only with reference to
the sub positions; he was speaking of the collectorship.

What I am objecting to is
that the hon. member was casting doubt in the minds pf the members of this House and. the people of this country as to whether I was adopting that policy in his own county. Yet, when there was a vacancy in Bathurst, right in his own county, I appointed a returned soldier who did not live in the county. The gentleman that he refers to was n.ot in the county at the time of the vacancy and I brought in a returned soldier from another county who had done duty in France, who was wounded and who is occupying that position in Bathurst at the present time. There you see that I was trying , tp follow out that policy in the county which the hon. gentleman represents. As far as the man to which the hon. gentleman refers is concerned, I have not heard anything of him and he has not made any application. I would like to ask the hon. member if his attention has been drawn to the fact that as soon as the Liberal party came into power in New Brunswick they dismissed every Conservative official in the whole province. One of the first was the sheriff right in the town of Bathurst who, as the hon. gentleman knows, was one of the best officials in the county, a man that they could not say one word against, a man who bad a son, or several sons at the front. Yet, they dismissed him without any investigation or anything else and they have not appointed a returned soldier to the position in New Brunswick. As far as* the appointment of a returned soldier to a position in New Brunswick, the situation is this:	Here is an official
who had been 15 or 16 years in office, a man that no one in the county could point his finger at, a man who took no part in political matters and yet he was hoisted out of his office the minute the Liberal Government came into power.
They did not appoint a returned soldier to the position. I have been asked, in view of the fact that no soldier, as the hon. members says, has returned from the front, in view of the many men who have gone from that county and the possibility of men coming back who might be injured to such an extent that they were not fit for any other occupation, a man with an arm or a leg off, or in view of the fact that the sons of this man who has been dismissed as sheriff of the county will probably return, perhaps invalided, whether I would not appoint him temporarily to that position until one of his sons came home or until some other man came home who would be able to fill it. This has been urged especially because of the fact that the Liberal government have taken the livelihood of a man 60 or 65 years of age by dismissing him in that way. I have refrained from appointing a returned soldier but in view of the fact that the Liberal Government in New Brunswick are dismissing officials without one word of warning, instead of following up the policy that I have been following with regard to the appointment of returned soldiers, I would ask my hon. friend, now that the matter has come up, if he thinks it would be an unfair thing to allow a man to act temporarily while his sons are at the front or until one of his sons, or some other man, comes back who is qualified to fill that position.

As to the appointments made by the Liberal Government of New Brunswick, I have no responsibility, although I will say to my hon. friend that if the son of that sheriff who has been dismissed, as he says, by the Liberal Government, were to return the first of them all, I would be in harmony with the minister for his appointment. Had he not mentioned the appointment of an assistant to the Customs Department of a returned soldier from outside of the county, I would not have mentioned this, because I had in mind simply the ensuring of the position now vacant for a returned soldier. As to the political conduct of the ex-sheriff, the man who has been dismissed, my hon. friend says he has never been an active politician. May I contradict him in that respect? I say that he has been a very active politician, active against myself in every election* since he was appointed until the last election when, a few days before, seeing the approach of a change of Government, he became very decent and quiet. At the same time if his son were to return-and' I

have a great respect for his son whom I know perfectly well-if he would be the first to return wounded or incapacitated and my hon. friend should be in power and give him the position, I would be in harmony with him.
I will give it to him anyway, whether you are ot not.

All right, we might give it to him. At the same time I want to say that I wanted to secure from the minister, after my hon. friend's reference to the postmastership in St. Thomas, where no doubt there are a great many returned soldiers, some guarantee for one of the returned soldiers in my county; and if the son of the dismissed sheriff should return, I would be satisfied with him or any one else the minister might appoint.

Would the hon. gentleman
consider it fair that, pending the return of his son who is now at the front, the dismissed Sheriff should be appointed temporarily to the position so that the son would have it on his return? Would the hon. gentleman agree to that?
I would agree to that.
You will agree to appointing the son?
Yes.
Then I will do it to-morrow.

He has a spn at the
front, and if he is appointed temporarily I accede to that.
If the hon. member agrees to that, I do not know his name, but tomorrow I will appoint him collector of customs and his father will go on and act until he returns.

See how quickly my hon. friend can change. Less than three minutes ago he was going to make the appointment whether my hon. friend agreed or not, and in less than three minutes he bases his appointment of the soldier on the agreement of my hon. friend. I wanted to ask the minister about conditions in his own constituency. The regulations to which I refer may perhaps come under some other department, possibly the Department of Immigration, but as the minister told us that he was the patronage committee in his own riding, he will understand the matter. I received a letter to-day saying that the international regulations under which men 
of military age are not allowed to cross between the United States and Canada were practically ignored between Prescott and Ogdensburg, down where my hon. friend lives. I know there is a good deal of traffic there, but I can scarcely believe that the situation can be as described in the letter I have received. If it is, then there is one port in Canada where the young men of Canada can practically go without restraint to the other side of the line. I should like an explanation from the minister.
I should like to say that I read an item that has appeared in the press that I had gone to Prescott-
I did not see that, it was some letters to me.

When I returned home on Saturday morning I had to leave for New York on Saturday afternoon, and when I went to the ferry dock there was a complaint there that those wishing to go across the river between the ages of 18 and 45 had serious difficulty with one of the immigration officials who had interpreted the Order in Council, or the instructions, to mean that' no one between the ages of 18 and 45 was to be allowed to cross. The other two officers interpreted the regulations as meaning that they were to be allowed to cross if they had the proper permits. The difficulty arose when the officer who thought that there was a total prohibition of crossing by those of military age was on duty. I explained to the one official that the interpretation of the others was the correct interpretation, and that unless the officers really felt that a man was trying to get away out of the country to escape military service, any man having the proper permit should be allowed to cross, as the Government desired to cause the least possible inconvenience. After that I understand there was no difficulty.
Do the photographs of these men accompany the permits?
Not in any that I saw.
Of course, the difficulty about the permits without a photograph need not be explained.

The difficulty was more with the local traffic. Men were coming from Brockville, Cardinal, Kemptville and other places back in the country, really between the two counties, and that is where the trouble arose. There did not seem to be any general complaint. I asked the customs officers if they had noticed any trouble,

and they said there was no difficulty at all. I think the whole trouble was there, as at many other ports, that the o.fficers were a little afraid, that they had not yet become accustomed to the working of the regulations. I do not anticipate trouble.
The minister has referred to the (payment of overtime to customs officials. What are the official hours for customs officers in country ports', and do the same hours apply to all country ports?

The regular hours are from
9 to 5. The officials are given overtime pay for work performed outside of those hours.
What is the rate for overtime pay?
Thirty cents an hour.
Would it not be better for the minister to do away with this overtime system and increase the salaries to provide for the extra work done?

This system has been in
force for a long time. I really do not think that the officials would favour the suggestion made by my horn, friend. In my town the men go on at 7 in the morning and work until 5 or 6. The ferry boats run until 12 midnight, and the men take turns in doing the overtime work. I think, then fore, that it would not toe practicable to place the salaries at such a high amount as to provide for the overtime. The salaries, including overtime, run from $1,200 to $1,300 per annum; the hours are not very long. If we abolished the overtime altogether, we should have to increase the staff, because ordinarily the men would be ev ployed only during the regular hours. In the town of Prescott about $2,000 a year is paid toy way of overtime. Ilf two more men were put on to take up the work otherwise done outside the regular hours, you would simply be taking it from the other men. Altogether, the system works very well.

What I suggest is that instead of paying the men extra for overtime, a fair wage he arrived at and paid as a stated salary. The .adoption of such a system would save much bookkeeping and much timekeeping. I do not know whether or not the men keep their own time, but if they do, they are all human, and they are apt to be not very strict as to the length of their overtime service. I should think that it would save much
bother and be muoh more satisfactory generally if the overtime payments were abolished and the salaries increased tp coveT work after hours.

The men would not work overtime if they received a regular salary; they would work from 9 to 5. As I say, the system has been very satisfactory, and I should not like to make any change without consulting the officials and going into the matter very thoroughly.
The minister did not answer my question as to whether the system of overtime applies to all ports.
It applies to ahy port where a man is employed outside the regular hours.

In his anxiety to attack the governement in the province of New Brunswick because of a question asked by the member for Gloucester, the minister a few moments ago charged the present Government of the province of New Brunswick with discharging every Conservative official in the province. For the purpose, I suppose, of offering an excuse for the manner in which he has carried on the affairs of his department in the interests of his own party, he makes this assertion against the Government of the province of New Brunswick. May I ask my hon. friend upon what information he bases the assertion which he has made, and what were the names of the persons dismissed?
That report has been in circulation since the present provincial Government came into power. The hon. gentleman can get sufficient evidence of that without asking me for it.
The minister has not any.
I may tell the minister that I have not any such information.

Yes, and I was there during the election. I had occasion to be at different polling booths in two different counties. At one of the places I attended a number of officials stood at the polls and worked against the government-and they are still holding office. The only evidence my hon. friend gave of officials being dismissed in the province of New Brunswick was the statement concerning the sheriff of the county of Gloucester. I may tell my



hon. friend that no sheriff has been dismissed in the province of New Brunswick since the election. The sheriffs in that province are appointed annually. In some cases the old sheriffs are reappointed; in other cases they are replaced because they have outlived their usefulness. During an election in the province of New Brunswick the registry office in a certain county was closed up to ordinary business and used as a Tory consulting room on election day. On another occasion a sheriff of a certain county established a polling booth in the Conservative committee room. My hon. friend had no justification for making the charge that he did against the Government of the province of New Brunswick, because the sheriff to whom he referred was not reappointed to office after his term had expired.

That matter has been
settled by the minister appointing to the office a gentleman recommended by the hon. member for Gloucester. I was going to suggest to the minister that as at least some of us have worked very faithfully, we should pass the first item, although it is a large one, and then adjourn. Of course, we shall be allowed to discuss almost any matter on the other items?

Certainly.
Progress reported.
